topic: The ability to think creatively and communicate possibilities will be reflected upon.
situation: We had to decide upon an innovative yet functional RGM theme.
task_action: Assignments were set out sequentially by weeks, with certain tasks concerning the RGM theme requiring a high level of creative thinking. The RGM theme needed to be completed by the week 3 workshop, hence a pre-workshop meeting was needed to brainstorm ideas. Whilst tutors recommended completing a LinkedIn Learning course on group ideation, I didn’t complete this till after the pre-meeting. During the brainstorm session we set up a Miro board with the topics ‘theme’, ‘events’, and ‘materials’, allocating coloured sticky notes to put ideas up for each part. Approximately an hour was spent completing this process and therefore a large quantity of ideas were produced. We proceeded to present these theme ideas back in our week 3 workshop, highlighting the theme concepts we were more interested in however not a singular theme. Following the creation and presentation of our problem statements in the subsequent week 4 workshop, we had the task of refining our problem statement to be more connected with our theme as well as producing a conceptual design for the week 5 workshop. Both required a definite theme, which our group had not decided upon. Our pre-workshop meeting for week 5 was allocated to refining our week 3 theme brainstorm into one theme. This was done by each individual selecting 2 ideas they liked in order to lower the quantity. Breakfast was a favourite however it was a common theme amongst other groups. Hence to be more creative we conducted a small 10 minute brainstorm session to communicate other possible meal times (e.g lunch and dinner) and how we could do a theme around them. We continued to then refine these ideas for the remainder of the session.
result: We were able to form 3 key themes surrounding meal times such as breakfast, lunch and dinner. We performed a group vote where a unanimous decision was in favour for the theme I had presented, an RGM to set up a dinner date for a couple. Thus we were able to tailor our problem statement to the theme, and begin our conceptual design.
pfr: REFLECTION Brainstorming an RGM theme seemed very distant to me initially, where I didn’t know how to go about it and thus left the challenges of it for the future. Additionally I had misunderstood the theme as something similar to a party theme (e.g superhero or hawaiian themed) rather than an overall function. This led to my concealed confusion in our brainstorm session on the theme, as I was too concerned with coming off as ignorant to people I had only recently met. As teammates kept posting theme ideas, I was hesitant in producing theme ideas and often found that the contributions I made were heavily refined. Watching my teammates as well as other groups present, my confusion was cleared as to what a theme for the RGM was. Our next group ideation session concerning the theme again in week 5 felt much more comfortable to me. I had completed a course on group ideation and thus brought in a more open attitude when we were attempting to communicate new ideas for our definite theme. The brainstorm session we had during week 5 had a shortened period 10 minutes plus a refining process shortly after. This was more effective opposed to the hour brainstorm as we didn't waste time stuck in a plateau and instead were able to use this time refining ideas. As we were looking for a theme surrounding a meal, I was thinking of a dinner date which I also thought would come off as ridiculous and laughable to the others. However by this time I had become more comfortable with my team and was less concerned with them viewing me as ignorant, thus I suggest the idea to which they all latched onto almost instantaneously. As a team we continued to suggest humorous ideas (such as having a male team member dressing as the girl date), which showcased my new found comfort, confidence and trust in myself and my teammates.
learning: By approaching situations with an open mind, creativity can flourish. The most detrimental factor to my communication of possibilities was my enclosed mindset. I had prioritised looking intelligent over presenting unrefined ideas, leading to my lack of involvement in our initial brainstorming sessions. After completing a course on group ideation and reflecting upon my own habits, I was able to eliminate my fear of being criticised within my group. Presenting unrefined and original ideas are the goal of a brainstorming session, as merely suggesting a raw concept to your group can ignite more solutions as a collective. Thus I have developed my ability to think creatively and communicate possibilities through my experience as of late.

topic: Dealing with different personalities and communication styles within a team.
situation: We needed to develop a team communication style which allows all members to contribute maximally in accordance with their unique strengths.
task_action: Completing DISC and OCEAN personality tests and discussing the results with the team, we became aware of the personality traits of each team member. We then compiled a team charter which assessed our strengths, weaknesses and goals to allow us to collaborate effectively and assume roles consistent with our skills and personalities.
result: We were able to consider the different styles of each team member before undergoing the design process, and we were able to assign roles based on individual skillsets.
pfr: Throughout weeks 1-6 of this project, the primary course for improvement in overall project planning and management lies in the communication between team members. We have encountered some issues involving efficiency and planning. This has impacted the delivery of our design, both from a group cohesion perspective and a timing perspective. This has also impacted the ability of individual team members to set themselves tasks with which to continue on. Before embarking on this project, I underestimated the importance of assigning clear roles to each team member, as well as scheduling set tasks. The way our team has navigated this has been suboptimal, with 2-3 people tending to run each team meeting, doing all the talking and setting all of the tasks. While this team dynamic does not inherently endanger the project outcomes, we have not been able to optimise workflow and communication by assuming this role due to some of our team members being left behind with little opportunity for contribution. Each team member has characteristics which affords them an opportunity to add a unique and personal touch to the project. Until this point, we have relied on the leadership skills of 2-3 team members to propel the project, without much consideration for other team members who may not be so inclined to readily offer their ideas. The group “leaders”, myself included, could have done a much better job of intentionally including the less talkative team members when brainstorming and planning.
learning: It has become apparent during the design phase that the quieter team members have their own valuable skillsets as we have reached the point where there are detailed tasks assigned to each person. Upon seeing the results from these tasks, I am inspired to re-think the way we navigated the initial team-building tasks. If I had taken the DISC and OCEAN tests more seriously, as well as the strengths and weaknesses sections of the team charter, it could have greatly improved our team dynamic, as well as the team’s overall functionality as it would have been clearer where each person’s unique skills lie. In addition, a more in-depth analysis of these activities would have allowed us to adjust our team plan to cater for a broader range of communication styles. As someone to whom a leadership/organisational role comes easily, I should have made a greater effort to ask individual team members for their contributions, instead of leaving discussions up to only those inclined by opening up each question to the whole group. In addition to assisting with future projects at university, these strategies will help me perform at my best in my future career, as well as in my personal life. Clear communication and awareness of the strengths of different personality types are crucial aspects of all kinds of relationships, and have an outsized effect on project outcomes and personal satisfaction.

situation: During week five our group brainstormed our conceptual design for the Rube Goldberg Machine (RGM) which would involve various modularized systems culminating in pressing the space bar on a laptop.
task_action: Using the problem definition from the previous group meeting, we identified the design constraints for our RGM machine: each member creates two unique events with each lasting a minimum 3 seconds, each event flows seamlessly to the next, materials are supplied using household items and the total system lasts a maximum 5 minutes. Next, we established the sequence of system in terms of member, who has initiating system and who finishes the system. Subsequently, we brainstormed various ideas and systems we could use for different events such as dominoes, pulley systems, ramps, balls/marbles, tubes, fans and so on. From there, we collectively brainstormed variations how each item/idea could be implemented in an event. Once all the suggested ideas were thoroughly assessed, each idea was ranked against different variations in terms of feasibility given time constraint, complexity, and uniqueness.
result: The result was collectively selecting 10 conceptual ideas from the list of 20 ideas brainstormed. Further, two mechanisms were given to each member depending on their assigned position within the RGM system to maximise a seamless transition between each event. This was done collectively after the team discussed and assessed each idea in various positions along the RGM machine.
pfr: Initially, I felt we as a team would get carried away with the brainstorming activity because the design parameters are very broad. I felt we would get too creative with our ideas to stand out to the point where the feasibility and reliability of design will be questioned. Additionally, I felt we were spending too much time on coming up with ideas due to creative freedom of the project. However, this easily resolved by limiting the brainstorming ideas to 20. From here, we methodically narrowed the 20 ideas to 10 through a voting system based on creativity and feasibility given the time constraint. Subsequently, we assigned two ideas to each team member depending on their position in the sequence of the machine and materials they had home to construct that idea.
learning: Through this, it was evident that attacking any obstacle regardless of size and scope in a systematic manner is paramount. By first establishing the main objective and the relevant parameters involved it allows gives the team clarity and direction given the time constraint. Further, by involving all members of the team through brainstorming it encouraged a greater creativity within the design process and using a voting a system to decide on design plans made all the team members feel inclusive and contributory. As such, it allowed us as a team to create the best design possible in line with the requirement. Hence, my appreciation and understanding of creative thinking and importance of setting goals has heightened.

topic: Reflection on “Forming effective teams” and “The design process phasing and approaches” and how these contribute to each other.
situation: Throughout the first 5 weeks of Eng1050, as part of team C15 we’ve been through the first few stages of engineering design including brainstorming, conceptual design, and preliminary designing. Becoming acquainted with my teammates, Nathan, Keith, Jake, and Rita has been a rewarding and new experience and has opened my eyes to the importance of teamwork in an engineering setting
task_action: We’ve been tasked to design and create a Rube Goldberg Machine under certain restrains and within a time limit. The machine has 10 separate events, 2 for each person, within a 13-week period (by the end of the semester) As a group we first needed to becoming familiar with each other through the use of some ice breakers and working together on our ENG1050 project. Through the use of Miro and Zoom Whiteboards, we have successfully completed our brainstorming and conceptual designs to a satisfactory standard. We have also begun the preliminary design phase, designing and finalising what we are planning to build for our RGM and the materials required.
result: The brainstorming included our problem definition, theme, and events of our RGM. Our problem definition is “Create an RGM with strict criteria (including materials and rubric) and time sensitivity (13 weeks)”. Our theme is “trash/garbage” to fit in with our material restrictions. As a team we thought that since we could only use items found around the house we would try to stick to this theme. The events have been a major accomplishment so far for our team, creating a system of flowing events in the RGM that we believe would work the best with each other. We also use a rotating system of roles, including chair, minute taker, and presenter to let everyone try different aspects of team roles and to build a more effective team, highlighting strengths and weaknesses of each team member.
pfr: Forming a team and employing engineering design processes and approaches has proven to be an exciting yet daunting challenge as a first-year engineer. In the beginning, our group struggled with awkwardness and didn’t know how to communicate. Personally I've always struggled with getting myself part of a group and preferred to work alone. However, through determination and many workshops together as I team I realise how important teamwork is. We have gotten to know each other very well and are enjoying the challenge of using engineering design processes to fulfil our final project goals, making it a fun and rewarding experience. Using the information provided on iLearn along with our creativity and dedication, my team has begun exploring the engineering design processes and are steadily tracking towards our end goal of a completed RGM. The brainstorming process has been a major struggle as we had so many ideas yet no clear direction or theme within them to progress with. As a team we worked through this challenge and landed on a single theme and events to go along with that theme. Then through the conceptual design phase we went through a range of events and how they could pair together to create a flowing machine. Some events were simply not feasible, so we decided not to go with them, and other events did not connect well so we had to rearrange the order of these events.
learning: Overall I’ve learnt that working within a team, especially with complete strangers is definitely a challenge, but having an end goal and the motivation to push each other toward that goal can lead to amazing friendships and enjoyable sessions together. When faced with an engineering challenge its important to follow each step of the engineering design process thoroughly to create the best outcome for a completed design. Although the initial problem definition and conceptual designs I thought to be initially very easy steps turned out to be quite challenging especially in a group with conflicting ideas. But, to work together as a team and decide on the best ideas to put forward is the amazing part of teamwork and through the engineering design process becomes quite trivial. Although I thought the first few steps of the design process were useless and wasted time, I’ve come to realise that they are the essential foundation to any engineering problem and are the key to a successful solution. I also need to put more faith into my teammates. I am always worried about the quality and work ethic of those around me, and when I want something done correctly I find myself taking over as I trust myself to do most things to a high quality, however through this engineering problem I found I need to let that go and to be able to put trust into others to contribute their part to the end goal. We are a team after all, and everyone in my group is capable of producing high quality engineering solutions, I need to let my ego go.

task_action: We met for the first time over zoom at a Friday workshop in the first week of the semester. The only information we had that week was that we needed to form an effective team, assign roles, values, goals and expectations moving forward. We subsequently learnt in the following weeks that as a team we would need to design, build and present a Rube Goldberg Machine by the end of the semester. This task required us to form an effective and efficient team to complete the project to a high standard and within the given timeframe. We discussed our goals for the project and what values we would hold each other accountable to. It was agreed that we needed to meet and have a team bonding session.
result: In the first week, we broke the ice and got to know each other as individuals. We created a WhatsApp group, a shared google drive and started a Miro page to brainstorm ideas. There was an overall agreement that in order to be a successful team, we needed to become comfortable in communicating with each other openly and honestly. With this in mind, we all met in person on campus within a week of the first meeting and played some games of pool as a team bonding exercise. This enabled everyone to have a laugh, learn more about each other and create a comfortable relaxing environment to work in. Through that experience, a regular Tuesday zoom meeting was established and an effective team was developed. We quickly fell into a rotating roster and agreed that each person should change roles every week to share the workload.
pfr: At first I felt somewhat nervous and a small amount of anxiety before meeting my team members. I was worried and unsure as to how each member would act and as to what their level of commitment would be towards the project. Those concerns were mostly quashed after the initial meeting. I tried to be as open and friendly as possible, including making jokes whilst attempting to make it a fun experience for everyone. I think this helped at certain stages to calm the group and remove any tension or uncertainty. Upon leaving the team bonding exercise, I was very confident that we had an effective team and that each member had the correct mindset moving forward. We continue to be an effective team and have fallen into our rotating roster smoothly which gives me a very positive outlook for the rest of the semester.
learning: The attitude and the positive mindset that each member brought to the group made it very easy to form an effective team. I understand that if each member had not come with a committed attitude, it may have been much harder to achieve this goal. We all agreed from the outset that constant communication and a respectful environment is key to working efficiently. I have learnt that a team bonding exercise in the right setting with the right mindset can do wonders in forming an effective team. Creating that close knit and friendly environment as well as the understanding that we're there to achieve the best we can is immeasurably good for any team environment. This experience has also taught me that understanding each persons role within the team is very important in the productivity of meetings and achieving goals each week.

situation: We needed to brainstorm a design mechanism through weeks 1-6 for the creation of the Rube Goldberg machine which involves dropping a Berocca tablet into water. The tablet falls out of its vessel and undergoes various complex situations and processes until it finally falls into water and dissolves.
task_action: We went through various brainstorming sessions throughout the weeks and came up with the Berocca tablet idea for the RGM. Our group came up with a problem statement for this idea, which was that the Berocca tablet cures headaches, releases energy, reduces tiredness, and helps support immunity, which would help a university student get through university. situation: In week three of our workshop for ENGG1050, we as a group brainstormed of ways to conceptually design a Rube Goldberg Machine that would consist of a minimum of 10 action events with each action event lasting 3 seconds minimum.

The first flawed solution being to make a software that simulates the actions of the machine, but due to the complexity of creating such a software and questions as to whether it violates any of the constraints presented by the problem, the idea was abandoned. The second idea was for each of us to design two action events and that we would later physically compile those action events into one machine, but this idea was also flawed as one member wouldn’t be able to participate in the physical creation of the machine and would have to burden other group members with the responsibility of physically creating the individual’s design.
result: After researching some more, we came to the conclusion that each individual member would be responsible for creating and recording a video of a working version of our Rube Goldberg machine consisting of 2 action events and that the ending of each action event would be a transition from one group member’s video to the other member’s. Through video editing, we would make it seem as one complete Rube Goldberg machine that at the time satisfies most of, if not all the constraints presented by the task.
pfr: Currently being a student geographically studying in Bangladesh and having to communicate and work with students located in Australia was definitely a frightening task for me initially to say the least. As a result of those prior experiences, I was not excited to work in a group, but after meeting up with my team members, I am happy to say that I am satisfied with my team as each member is willing to take responsibility and work on their own actions. Furthermore, being the only member that is currently not located in the same geographical area meant that for the physical construction of the machine, I would have to heavily rely on my other team members and possibly delegate most of my responsibilities onto someone else. learning: Finally, through brainstorming as a team, we were able to find a solution that all group members were satisfied with. As long as we met the constraint requirements, we decided that the conceptual design of creating our own two events and transitioning into one another’s was the most suitable one for our current situation. I was able to learn through rational decision making approaches and effective team communication, that we as a team could come up with a solution that not only holds the team accountable for their respective operations, but also able to create an effective and efficient solution where each team member would be able to maximize on their own strengths and minimize on their own weaknesses by taking on the responsibility of creating their own action events, where we wouldn’t have to rely on anyone else’s knowledge or resources, but also be able to communicate and share our expertise if one of us needs it. topic: Trade-offs, judgment, and balance in resolution
situation: During the making of my stages in the RGM I discovered that working with dominoes was harder than I thought.
task_action: I began working on my sections; a spiral ramp on which a circular object would roll down and hit a piece of domino and start the chain reaction of falling dominoes. Initially I planned to make the domino chain loop 2 times around my spiral ramp. However very quickly I discovered while arranging the dominoes that when I made a mistake; perhaps my hand slipped or I shook the table I was working on too roughly or I didn't get the spacing right, the whole domino chain would fall and I would have to make it all from scratch again. I did this about 8 times and quickly realized the longer I made the domino chain the more fail points there were in the system and the more stuff I would have to rebuild when it failed.
result: I decided to make the domino chain only loop around my ramp 1 time which drastically reduced the amount of dominoes used and therefore the amount of failure points however it made it less impressive as well.
pfr: At the time I was feeling very frustrated because it took me 2 hours to build and fail then rebuild and fail then rebuild… and so on. I must have built the domino chain 8 or 9 times. And after all of that, when I realized I had to compromise if I wanted to get it done in any realistic time frame and therefore make it less impressive than I initially wanted it to be, I was very frustrated. But when I made the chain smaller and finally got it right I came to the conclusion that the compromise was a wise decision.
learning: When confronted with the fact that sometimes what you have in mind doesn't quite work out as well as you hoped in real life, it can be very frustrating and disappointing. And you have to make a decision on whether you want to proceed with your original plan despite the difficulties or compromise. And if you do decide to compromise, by how much? It's a careful balancing act of trying to make as much of your idea a reality as realistically as possible.

topic: Initiative and the willingness to make decisions in the face of uncertainty
situation: During week 4 of the project, we started to work on our RGB design concept. During brains storming process of the project design, we were advised not to limit our imagination and let out creativity work at full and come up with as many ideas as possible no matter how unrealistic they could seem.
task_action: It was interesting to discuss a project with no limits in terms of design, however, the situation at this stage was uncertain. We didn’t know what kind of difficulties we can encounter in the future building RGB machine, and at that stage, it was already clear that our group has some credibility, attendance, and contribution issues. Aiming to avoid difficulties with deadlines I suggested choosing the simplest design so we could compensate if someone wasn't able to complete their task on time.
result: As a result, we came up with a simple solution that still complied with the project requirements and constraints. By now I can say that in a long run it was a very rational decision.
pfr: The decision to create the simplest design was based on my previous group project experience during ENGG1000. In a similar situation, our group overcomplicated the initial design by not thinking ahead. Short time, neglecting duties by some group members, and the amount of work due to project complexity put our project at risk of not being done on time. This time I didn’t want to be in the same situation. I was optimistic about our team’s capability and dedication at the beginning until it became clear that not everyone is willing to put effort into group work. Watching other’s group presentations, I was impressed by how complex and creative their RGB projects were. At this point, I started to doubt if we made the right decision. Inspired by others I thought maybe we should change direction and make our project more creative. But reality brought me back to the initial plan. I think there are no limits to what can be created as long as there is a strong team working together hard toward the aim. Being in a situation where half of the team is not enthusiastic about a project, I think the best choice was to keep it simple in order not to put extra work on the rest of tee team.
learning: I can’t say that I learned something new from this situation because I’ve already experienced it before, and what I’ve learned from the past contributed to the decision-making process this time. Besides personal traits that could draw a team back, there are always other commitments and unexpected situations that anyone can experience, so occasional team members’ absence or lack of participation should always be taken into account when working on a design and construction. It might be not applicable to a working place due to different conditions but in a situation where I have to work in a team with randomly chosen members for a short period of time, I would make it a rule for myself: start low and slow and add complexity if time allows, rather than start with something complicated and not be able to finish it on time because human factor has not been considered.

topic: I'm reflecting over the skill of adaptability when applying theoretical ideas in a practical setting.
situation: In this class, we had to design a physical process (Rube Goldberg Machine) over the virtual medium of Zoom, and were therefore unable to actually design it with exact physical considerations.
task_action: My team and I used Miro, Lucidchart and Zoom whiteboard to design the series of events for the RGM, however until we got together in person we were unable to accurately account for all physical factors. Once we did meet and attempted to construct the RGM, we were met with problems such as the ball bouncing too far off some events due to the solid wood tables we used for the foundation. To resolve issues such as these, we had to modify the elements on the fly, for instance, we replaced a mini basketball with a cricket ball to make it more weighted when the former wouldn't work, or when we adjusted the locations of the bumpers for the second event.
result: We managed to complete the construction and filming for the first 7 events in a single attempt, and the next 3 were done a week later, without too much adjustment to the actual plan and while achieving basically the same result. Being adaptable and using improvisational solutions allowed us to save time in the design process but meant that nothing was lost in the actual design.
pfr: Originally, the whole process of creating an RGM online without a physical design space seemed overwhelming and impossible. If we stayed fixated on the idea of 'perfection' despite being unable to work in it while planning, we would not have been able to make progress. However, since we were adaptable we managed to sort out the minor problems we encountered throughout the physical design process, and the major issues we encountered were resolved similarly.
learning: Being able to be adaptable meant we got the project done in time and had plenty of time to create the presentation and work on the rest of the unit's work. We saved a large amount of time and ended up coming with a greater range of ideas, as we were not stuck in with a singular mindset and could make do with what we originally planned while still doing with what we had available. As a point of learning, the ability to improvise and be adaptable is a valuable skill that I will be putting into use in the future.

topic: Effectiveness of Oral Presentations within remote learning - Oral Presentation
situation: In my example, the experience recently took place at the Macquarie University within the context of a team/group project that is directed towards the Rube Goldberg Machine. This project was undertaken as part of an Engineering unit (ENGG1050 - Engineering Design). My team consisted of six team members, including myself. As a key part of the development of professional identity and personal development, us students were required to participate in weekly online workshop presentations. An effective presentation makes the best use of the relationship between the presenter and the audience. It takes full consideration of the audience’s needs in order to capture their interest, develop their understanding, inspire their confidence and achieve the presenter’s objectives. These presentations specifically involved a member from each group to present on weekly based objectives infront of other groups and an assigned tutor. In a nutshell, the weekly presentations were not only focused on the group's visual aspects, but also examined the oral presentation.
task_action: Undergoing weekly presentations, for week's 7 presentation we were tasked with a team/group presentation consisting of 3 members from each group and restricted with the time constraint of 10 minutes per group. This presentation had to consist our group's complete detailed design and an in-depth discussion on how the individual scenes of our project led to a fulfilled Rube Goldberg Machine. As the name suggests, the task was to be completed through the use of several systematic diagrams to enable the audience to visually capture our group's RGM model. Consequently, through the use of 'Miro' and our schedule plan a week before the presentation submission, we allocated 3 members of our group to conduct the presentation for week 7. As a team we assigned and distributed the work evenly so that we could work at a fast pace and also have fair contribution towards the project itself. This was by the means of having 3 presenters to create the visual presentation and an oral script. Whilst, the rest of the team members were tasked to achieve the weekly objective which was to construct the detailed design of our RGM model.
result: The result of this situation was being able to present our group presentation and also meeting our weekly objective for week 7. In our viewpoint, we strongly believe that due to our presentations being commenced online, this gave us less room to engage and interact with the presentation overall. We are also of the opinion that a good presentation should be concise and should be focused on the topic. It should not move off-track. Essentially, this led up into the main context of the ‘effectiveness of oral presentations within remote learning’ and what makes the best use of the relationship between the presenter and the audience. We felt that it takes full consideration of the audience’s needs in order to capture their interest, develop their understanding from the early preface, inspire their confidence and achieve the presenter’s objectives. We also felt that 'Miro' was a great opportunity and addition to make working a lot more streamlined. situation: During the second half of the semester of ENGG1050, we have been tasked with developing and refining our individual components for the groups Rube Goldberg Machine. We utilised previous work to ensure timelines for our deliverables and used communication skills to compromise and find the best solutions to all our skills. There was the additional impacts on this portion of testing and validating our own work as workloads and requirements continually changed to chase reliability targets.
task_action: The Task was to create, by designing initial events, then refining, 2 events for a Rube Goldberg Machine which had to last at least 3 seconds in length. We created our first drafts independently and aligned with our Gantt chart to ensure we had enough time to draft and then present them for the next weeks presentation. We presented our drafts within the team and looked critically at our own and others to find possible flaws or errors in assumptions that led us to our draft designs. With these conversations we developed a better understanding of what we were targeting for designs and the metrics we’d use to measure how successful we were in them. This led us to complete our final design which in some cases were significantly closer to reality than others, this allowed us to take insight into how others constructed and pieced together their respective systems to trigger key events within the Rube Goldberg Machine.

learning: It’s been a major bit of learning my limits to be attached to my work, but to also work through and develop a refined problem solving mindset. While this will surely grow and develop more as I enter the workforce and encounter more varied issues that require even more varied skillsets, I am of the view that this exercise has also worked these mental muscles. Being an engineer means admitting when a solution simply doesn’t meet the requirements, or doesn’t pass the tests, and its a harsh reality but one we must all confront, by doing so now I can feel more confident in being able to manage my emotional response to it in future.

To do this I drew up a study plan which included a weekly checklist of the most important tasks for each of my five subjects. I also used a calendar board to visually display all due dates as well as when I should begin tasks, such as, assignments. task_action: To give some context about my events, I will describe them. In the last inclined plane from the previous event, a ping pong ball goes down the ramp from event 5 and it knocks over some coffee beans, into an empty cup connecting to another pulley system. Once the empty cup is filled with coffee beans, it weighs down a string and lifts a glass bottle on the other end of the pulley system. The end of the popsicle bomb has a few sticks that, if released, blow up the entire bomb. These sticks were stabilised by the glass bottle that was lifted off by the pulley system. At first, the only change that came to mind was that the cup was too unstable and did not have a wide enough surface area to catch the coffee beans so, the cup was replaced with an open drawstring bag, which had a wider opening, and would potentially the coffee beans better. However, when I tried to actually implement my events, I realised there were many flaws in the design. It was extremely difficult to get all the loose beans into the drawstring bag, and the glass bottle was not heavy/sturdy enough to keep the popsicle stick bomb in place without prematurely exploding. The ping pong ball was also too light to hit the coffee bag. Fortunately, by using my creativity and problem-solving skills, I was able to make use of other materials that were available around me to solve each and every problem I was facing and end the day with my final video.
result: I broke down the problems I was facing and tried to solve them one at a time. The first issue was the drawstring bag being too light, causing it to move about a lot from the position that would be ideal to catch the coffee beans. I looked around the Ada Lovelace room at 4RPD, and found a MQ goodie bag in the cupboard, which was way more stable and stayed in place. The coffee beans would spill everywhere, so to improve the repeatability and a higher chance of success, I decided to drop a bag of coffee rather than individual coffee beans. At times, the coffee bag would slide sideways down the cardboard ramp. To stabilise that, I taped a long wooden stick under the ramp, making it a lot more sturdy. I grabbed a big box from the cupboard and put it under the ramp, stabilising it further. The other issue was the glass bottle not being heavy enough, so I decided to fill it up with water. Those adjustments solved all the issues I was having with the design.

Resource management, understanding needs and setting goals.
situation: Throughout the duration of our mid-semester break, we were tasked with building and testing the Rube Goldberg Machine components that each of us were responsible for designing.
task_action: The task is for each individual member of our group to build the Rube Goldberg machine components consisting of 2 action events, with each action event lasting a minimum of 3 seconds and that our components must be modularized, where the ending of each action event would be a transition from one group member’s video to the other member’s. It’s important that each member supply their own material and keep sustainability in mind, where the resources that are used are recyclable or items that we already have in our possession.
result: After finding out ways to use the resources that were readily available to me more efficiently and effectively, I was able to not only create my RGM components but I was also able to make sure that the action events for each RGM component lasted for at least 3 seconds and that the beginning of the action event I was responsible for would transition from one of my group member’s video and that the ending of my action event would transition to another member’s RGM component. The first action event created was for a marble to go down a pipe and the second action event would be triggered by that same marble, where the marble initiated a domino effect where multiple CD boxes would topple over each other and the last CD box would trigger another marble to fall down which would transition to another rube Goldberg machine component created by another team member.
pfr: Personally, I’ve never created a mechanical device so the idea of creating something called a Rube Goldberg machine seemed very daunting to me. Even in high school, I’ve had very limited experience with experiments, where I haven’t even done something as basic as a carbonated soda volcano. So, from the start I felt like I had a weakness in terms of my inexperience with practical work. It was also initially a detriment to me where I kept trying to think of very sophisticated ideas in order to make sure that the action events lasted the bare minimum of 3 seconds, which probably would’ve required resources that wouldn’t have been available to me and skills that I hadn’t really developed. Upon further reflection, I realized that as long as I met the requirements of the project, using simple methods and adjusting the way that I use my resources for this specific case would be the best idea.
learning: When building and testing my Rube Goldberg Machine components I learnt that for someone who’s inexperienced with practical work as I am the simple ideas are the best and that there is no need to overly complicate matters. For instance, when I was trying to make the length of first action event longer, I was thinking of using different contraptions and machinations such as a pulley system along with my initial idea of a marble going down a pipe to make the action event longer. Upon reflection I realized that I just need to make it within the requirement of lasting 3 seconds, there was no benefit to intentionally making the event even longer than that, so I decided to simply increase the length of the pipe that I used to make sure the action event lasted the minimum of 3 minutes. I also had an initial reliability issue of where the CD boxes would fall on their own and were not stable enough to stand by themselves. Instead of replacing the boxes, I simply opened them slightly, which gave them a larger base, which in turn gave them more stability to stand up by themselves. By simply adjusting the way that I am using my resource, I conserved materials and increased the overall resource efficiency of the project. These actions have allowed me to understand the needs and requirements of my project and by simply adjusting the way I use my resources I can meet the goals that I have set for myself using effective resource management.

learning: By utilising critical thinking as a methodical-based approach to every problem, I was even able to solve the more complicated coding problems at the end of the skill allocation despite facing difficulties at beginning. Throughout this experience, I have formed a greater appreciation of critical thinking as it demonstrated to me how it is better to carefully analyse and evaluate several solutions and then choose the most appropriate one, rather than simply trying to solve the problem by essentially “brute forcing” your way through it. The key idea from this experience that I will be taking away into further engineering units and even my future career is how crucial critical thinking is in creating solutions to seemingly complicated problems, and how it is widely incorporated in many problems we encounter.

task_action: every week, we are given 3 hours to finish each lesson. These 3 hours are very important, because we are given special tools that allow us to draw with consistent angles and lengths. situation: The situation relating to time and resource management that I experienced was the 2 weeks leading up to my HSC (High School Certificate) final Year 12 exams in 2022 (these exams would determine my final mark and what degree I would qualify for accordingly). During this 2 week period I had my 18th birthday and I had my Year 12 formal party, so it became very difficult to balance studying and celebrating. The stress of the final exams was finally settling in and I was unable to enjoy these 2 major events that a person only gets to experience once. So whilst I wanted to fully enjoy my 18th birthday party and my Year 12 formal, the thought of the final exams was constantly lingering in the back of my mind. Hence, I had to find a way to manage my time such that I didn’t regret not enjoying these events but also not regretting that I didn’t study enough for the exams.
task_action: To ensure that I enjoyed my time during these 2 once in a lifetime events and also did my best in the HSC, I had to implement certain time and resource management strategies. It was through these strategies that I was able to achieve my task of maximising my efficiency whilst studying so that I would be able to spare time to enjoy my 18th birthday party and my formal. The very first step I took was to plan ahead, as time itself is also a vital resource. I utilised Google Calendar to break each day up into study sections. Each study section was 2 hours and I would focus upon a single subject. During these study sections I would either go through my flashcards using an app called Anki (which utilises the study technique called spaced repetition) or I would attempt practice exams and reattempt questions I got wrong. By reattempting questions I got wrong I was able to gain maximum benefits out of the practice papers which were limited. The next action I took was setting clear priorities. As the dates of each exam was spread out, I would spend more time on the subject that had its test the earliest. Next, I would prioritise topics within each subject whereby I knew I had gaps in my knowledge. This enabled me to not only reinforce what I knew but also ensure that I wasn’t going into my exams without knowing everything that I needed to. Another step that I took was to focus on one task at a time. Rather than thinking about each subject as a whole, I made a To Do list on Google Keep which enabled me to break the subject down into parts. This reduced the stress greatly as larger topics were broken down into more mentally digestible smaller topics. The final step that I took was setting shorter deadlines. For example I would aim to get at least 5 practice exams for a subject, 1 week prior to its exam date. This would ensure I was completing my work earlier than I should have. By doing so I was constantly ahead and on top of what I needed to study.
result: The objectives of my actions were to maximise the use of the little time I had to study for my exams so that I would be able to enjoy my 18th birthday party and my Year 12 formal party. The result of my actions was that I was able to fully enjoy the two events with only minimal effects on my exams. I had attempted each test to the best of my ability and I was confident that I was going to receive the mark that I wanted. I hadn’t regretted enjoying the parties or wishing that I spent more time studying for my exams. Moreover I had very little stress during my exam period. When I got my ATAR (final mark) back, I had achieved the goal that I had set. However I was certain that I could’ve done better by not attending the parties, but this didn’t bother me as I knew it would’ve had no extra benefit as I achieved the goal I wanted to. In the end, I had no regrets and I achieved the initial task that I had set out to complete.
pfr: Before I set out to efficiently study by utilising time and resource management techniques, I was quite overwhelmed with the workload and very stressed. This affected other areas of my life such as not exercising or eating properly. I was thinking that I was going to fail my exams, I would not get into the degree I wanted, that my future would be ruined and that I would not be able to enjoy my parties. However after implementing the strategies I was more confident than I had ever been about any exam I ever took. During the exams, I didn’t pay much attention to whether or not I had enjoyed my parties and my only focus was doing the best I could in the exam. However, after the exams I was content and joyful with what I had done, as I had not only done well but also enjoyed my parties.
learning: By utilising such time and resource management strategies I was able to achieve all the goals I had set out before the exams. I learnt that it was futile for me to be stressed before the exams because I should have been confident when I implemented the strategies. Moreover, I learnt how to fully maximise my time and organise tasks efficiently. I have been able to carry forward these skills into university and I have constantly been on top of my work with minimal stress. Through this experience I have learnt not only these vital time and resource management skills but also how to reduce stress and have a more positive mindset when faced with larger workloads.

situation: Product cost fluctuation makes it harder to arrange the balance between worker (supplier), middle man (transport), and final buyer (seller). We are the middle man, and we want to find a solution to guarantee our money because the price may change instantly after we buy from the supplier and the buyer may not offer the price that we want. We need to make a profit to pay for the labor, transportation costs, and future investments. What is the solution?
task_action: Making a brainstorm session; forming a discussion group involving everyone in the organization; writing down every suggestion on the whiteboard; encouraging everyone to be creative and contribute. After we make a mind map and identify any related ideas, we select the most feasible ones to turn a profit. The main success came from the fact that there was no hierarchy postulating solutions; everyone was included, so we gathered many ideas.
result: Solution 1: Suppliers prices are defined by the demand of the market. The possible solution to controlling the supplier price is to dominate the supplier market by producing a unique product. Solution 2: Let's say we pay certain money to the labor and to the trunk for one day; however, our job finished in 2 hours. We paid for 9 hours, but since we do not have a second supplier, our 7 hours money is basically wasted. The solution is to negotiate with other suppliers and convince them to sell their products at a reasonable price. Solution 3: Finally, we brought the product to the buyer, but the buyer changed the price to a lower price. The buyer was greedy; they wanted to make more profit. Solution is: Instead of begging them to purchase our product, we parked the trunk in front of the potential buyers and held an auction, and the highest bidder earned the right to buy the product. By doing this, we get into a more advantageous position. Solution 4: Another reason for the disagreement with buyers is that they do not know us because we are new in this market. They are right in that they are not sure about the quality of our product. The solution is to make ourselves known to them by preserving our high quality all the time. In addition to that, we always have those products, so when the demand increases, they will know that they can reach us and we can supply the demand. This trust will get stronger with time. Solution 5: In the long term, becoming the seller itself by building a platform Solution 6: Building a logistic center to encourage the small supplier to deliver their products Small suppliers will be compensated with a good price, so they will trust us that we are not taking advantage of them. Trust is the best advertisement, which spreads from ear to ear. It will make us more recognized in the industry. Solution 7: Exporting the product
pfr: When I found out that my business partner had lied to me and taken all the company's money, I felt a crushing mix of anger, disappointment, and disbelief. I had put all my trust in them, and the idea that they would break that trust was unthinkable. I felt violated on both a personal and a professional level, which made me doubt myself and question my ability to judge people.
learning: Even though this was painful and hard, it has taught me a lot of important things. First, I've learned how important it is to have clear legal agreements that spell out what each partner is responsible for and what they can expect from the other. This knowledge will help me stay out of trouble in the future. Second, I have a better understanding of how important it is to be honest and communicate openly in business relationships, as well as how important it is to review financial records and transactions regularly to make sure that people are held accountable. Also, this has shown how important trust and personal integrity are in business partnerships. Even though I can't control what other people do, I can make better decisions about who to work with in the future by doing a thorough background check on potential partners and getting feedback from people who have worked with them before. Going forwards, I will think about these lessons and change how I do business in the future. I will put a high priority on making clear legal agreements, putting in place systems for financial transparency, and making sure my partners can talk to me freely. Also, I'll be more careful and deliberate when picking business partners, paying close attention to their values and past performance. By using these tips, I hope to protect myself and my business from the potential pitfalls of betrayal and dishonesty and, in the end, build a more successful and trustworthy foundation for future projects.

The coding task that I assigned was chosen based on difficulty and topic that the student found was the hardest to understand.

The example the for, while and do loops that I selected where picked to be easy to understand such that the student could recognise patterns and be able to understand the correct structure format. The questions picked for the student do complete had challenging requirements that were designed to make them think about complex loop structures which ultimately worked to improve their ability to competently write loops in C. However, something that could have been improved on in my teaching method would have been to get my student to collaborate in a group with peers to discuss ideas. situation: I needed to create multiple variants of the game "Rock, Paper, Scissors" using the C programming language. These variants had to: * exponentially incorporate additional hand gestures; * utilise a unifying algorithm that could mathematically calculate the winner of a round in any given variant.
task_action: Engaging in the 'pattern identification' stage of computational thinking; brainstorming and discovering the relationships between the gestures. This involved identifying several key parameters: * The total number of gestures must be odd; * Each gesture must win against half of the other gestures, and lose to the remaining gestures.
result: The result was being able to order the gestures based on these parameters, so that a winner could be calculated using modular arithmetic. For example: Order: * Rock = 0 * Paper = 1 * Scissors = 2 * Spock = 3 * Lizard = 4 Assuming that: * N = number of gestures * A = player 1 choice * B = player 2 choice The following algorithm was born: (A - B + N) % N: * A result of 0 would determine the outcome as a tie; * An odd number would determine the victory of Player 1; * An even number would determine the victory of Player 2.
pfr: The task seemed impossible at first, because I didn’t think it was possible to use the same algorithm for any variant. Adding additional gestures created chaos in my mind, preventing me from thinking clearly about possible solutions. Once I broke the problem down into smaller pieces, I found that it was much easier to approach the task objectively and define a solution that satisfied the prescribed criteria.
learning: By breaking down the problem into smaller, manageable parts, I learned that it’s easier to define the solution through abstraction. I found a way to generalise an answer to a specific problem, by finding an answer to a more general problem. In doing so, I defined an efficient solution that could be applied to multiple variants of the game, avoiding needless repetition. Through this experience, I’ve come to appreciate optimal solutions that can be applied to multiple problems.

situation: After a lot of group work many tasks had been completed, many members of the group became rationally ignorant but did not ask for help. Workflow was being organised on a Trello Kanban board using cards.
task_action: The final stage of the civil modelling project involved documenting all work and assembling the concept model. Tasks were assigned by members to other members. I noticed that there was duplication in tasks with some tasks having already been completed. I acted to refocus the group activities and recommended members review the completed section on Trello.
result: Group members who were not highly engaged found it difficult to locate information on the Trello even though it was clearly labelled. I have concluded that for projects with Asymmetric member engagement of sufficient scale completed work must be migrated off the workflow space and into a documentation space such as confluence.
pfr: This sudden unexpected group disconnect at the late stage of the project was incredibly distressing. The fact that members felt they could no longer rely on the shared group interface caused the group cohesion to collapse and members to break off into individual work. The person assembling the concept model stopped communicating for days, the person tasked with annotating images thought the task was complete, the person laying out the presentation didn’t know what content was too be presented, the person laying out the document couldn’t get anyone to provide information he needed, and although I was busy assistance was never requested.
learning: Reliable stores of project documentation must be maintained to ensure all members share in the progress of all other members. Its obvious now, but I assumed all members were staying abreast of task progress when they were not. Usage of the project management tool “confluence” will be added to my group formation strategy (when the project is of sufficient scale or complexity that rational ignorance becomes a feasible outcome). For example, members should have been easily able to find the size of the building by searching project documentation without asking another member. The confluence will effectively act as a traceable project wiki of all generated information and files.

situation: Throughout my university experience I have had to learn how to take accountability for myself. During the Engg1050 RGM project, I have had to put my skills to the test and continuously refine them to ensure the success of both myself and my team members, with whom I have been actively collaborating.
task_action: I first started my academic career at UTS, where I studied for 2 years before I took a semester off due to an ADHD diagnosis. During my time at UTS, I had the opportunity to partake in four group projects, each with its unique set of group dynamics. It was during these projects that I initially began to develop my sense of accountability. As a student with ADHD, I face ongoing challenges in holding myself accountable, particularly with respect to tasks that require time management. This is the first group project I have been in since beginning my ADHD treatment and I have resolved to maintain my organisation and continue to enhance my sense of accountability. Since the initial workshop I have aimed to be a valuable member for my team. I took proactive steps, making a note of my team members names and reviewing their LinkedIn profiles to familiarise myself with their faces prior to meeting them. I took up position of team leader temporarily, ensuring that each member introduced themselves and that we had a platform to communicate outside of the scheduled workshop meetings. In preparation for our group sessions, I had established our Miro board and familiarised myself with the software in the event that none of my team members had done so. As it turned out, this was the case, and I took it upon myself to guide the team through the features of the platform and how to access our group board. Assuming the role of team leader, I was not only responsible for my own accountability, but also for the successful presentation of our team. I recognised the criticality of leadership and organisation for effective teamwork, and I committed to ensuring a seamless semester for our group. As the project progressed, I continued to fulfill the duties of team manager, even though I did not actively seek this role. However, due to the needs of the team, I remained in this position to ensure our collective success. Taking on the responsibility of organising a team in a group project requires the utmost accountability. Any oversights or failures on my part can potentially harm the team's progress and success. Additionally, it also means that I must hold others accountable for their responsibilities within the project, which can be challenging as a student, since I do not hold any formal authority. If I fail in this task, the completion of the work often falls to me. Throughout the project, I have consistently assumed responsibility not only for my own tasks but also for encouraging effective teamwork and communication. While I acknowledge that there is always room for improvement, I am committed to further developing my professional skills and enhancing my ability to take accountability for myself and future teams.
result: By taking accountability for my work and responsibilities I have successfully coordinated with my team, and we have managed to produce a high quality RGM design.
pfr: Taking accountability for ourselves is a hard task. It can be daunting to own up to our mistakes and you can be tempted to conceal them. Taking accountability requires self-awareness and honesty, shame or hurt pride in a failure is natural. However, by acknowledging those emotions and taking corrective action you can learn from your mistakes. By taking accountability you increase your self-awareness allowing you to see your role in the team and feel a sense of pride when your contributions aid in the team's success. Throughout this term, I have gained insight into the value of accountability, and its ability to enhance one's contribution to a team. This has empowered me to recognise the weight of my input and increased my self-esteem. Prior to this, I have encountered situations in which I felt unheard during group projects. However, through demonstrating a strong work ethic and reliability, I have earned the respect of my peers, which has allowed me to view myself in a more positive light.
learning: Through this course, I have gained insight into effectively managing my responsibilities, enabling me to consistently meet deadlines. Taking accountability has taught me valuable lessons that I can apply in both my personal and professional life. It has allowed me to become more self-aware and recognise my strengths and weaknesses. I have been able to identify areas in need of improvement and actively work towards refining my skills. It has also helped me to become more organised, manage my time effectively, and communicate better with my team members. Overall, taking accountability has allowed me to become a better team player and has improved my confidence in my abilities.

situation: As a first-year undergraduate student at Macquarie University, it’s been 6 weeks since I started grasping skills for unit ENGG1050 Engineering Design. So far, the class has been put into groups to implement a Rube Goldberg Machine for a project concerning 12 key events of 30 seconds duration. My experience with Team A12 has been nothing but exemplary since the weekly presentation and professional documentation of the meeting's agenda and minutes require a constant rotation of roles in the Team Charter. Looking back, I have had to take up the role of Minute-Taker twice and I’m not complaining since it’s a given that tasks are assigned based on the group member’s availability. However, when accepting a role, it is very important to get things done on time. The tutor-in-charge for our team has advised that it is recommended to turn in assessments before Tuesday night. Although records till week 2 show due dates having gone past Friday, it is a student’s responsibility to be aware of the content details provided in the unit guideline. I observed that procrastination is a problem that I am faced with and it took a hit on team morale. The matter at hand became worse when the Minute Taker for week 5 didn’t come through on their end. Absences were noted and hence there was nothing much to report for said person. For ENGG1050 Workshop, I had to take the initiative to do a presentation for the same week since the team member responsible for it had personal matters to attend to. Although a failed attempt, it also gave me a chance to learn that prepared speeches go a long way. The technical difficulties I faced during that time made me a bad candidate for the Presenter role.
task_action: Procrastination is a very bad habit for group assessments as one member's contribution could help to complete the given role of others. Back in year 10 high school, there was a task based on the recent Biology zoo excursion the class had to submit in writing. A group of three consisted of a Note-taker, Report-writer and Key-note Presenter. At the time, I was assigned to write the report but both of my friends were busy cramming for the upcoming Business Studies Exam. In the end, I had to stay up all night to prepare a PowerPoint Presentation as well. I want to avoid putting one of my team members in that kind of tough spot. Having to stay up all night is not a nice experience. So, it was decided that the Chairman role for Team A12 will also have the burden of supervising the shared Google Docs and Slides. To be targeted with deadline notifications in the group chat is rather motivational in its embarrassing way. The issue of absence led to the idea of choosing a Sub-Presenter for the Workshop Zoom Meetings. An alternate option of one person doing the slides while the sub-in prepares a speech has concurred. In case of an emergency, minutes-taking will be divided among all five members. Although not disclosed in Team Charter, a position for Group Leader is elected every week on a rotational basis. The person is then asked to update the Agenda Status while directing topics for future meetings. If a situation were to arise, even if inconvenient, they should be willing to take up the challenge.
result: For week 6, I noticed that Team A12 has had over three meetings outside of the Workshop hours. All meetings were initiated by the Group Leader while she conveyed that Preliminary Design Diagrams for the RGM events be posted up on the Google Slides created. situation: My team was tasked with creating a Rube Goldberg Machine (RGM) of our choice. The goal was to complete a simple task using multiple complicated tasks in a chain reaction. Each member would have 3 sections in the RGM and needed to have at least one unique element that was not present in another team members’ section.
task_action: We began with some basic research and taking inspiration from other RGMs that we saw on YouTube. This helped our understanding of our task and helped start the conversation around our brainstorm of our own unique ideas. We came up with a variety of tasks that are usually simple, such as making breakfast and getting ready in the morning. These simple tasks can be made more complicated to fulfil the requirements of a RGM. The other aspect of our task was to ensure we had a unique idea, so after seeing similar ideas from other groups, we had a further team brainstorm. Our new task was to complicate the simple task of making breakfast, but with a unique twist of using one of our team member’s pets. We approached the development of our RGM by breaking down the process into little steps, constantly thinking outside the box to make our RGM unique and stand out from the other groups. We all contributed to each other’s sections coming up with a range of creative ideas such as using our own pets in the RGM as well. For example, one member would use their birds by giving them food to eat off a plate which will lighten it and release a hot wheels car. I could use my cat by pointing a laser onto a button causing my cat to press it, activating an Arduino. The end result would be for the dog to receive treats, water and its favourite toy. I constantly encouraged and motivated my team to express their ideas no matter how big or small and I elaborated on their ideas in a respectful way, and encouraged them to be creative. I actively listened and provided positive feedback and suggestions to build on their ideas.
result: Ultimately, through the use of creative thinking skills and effectively communicating our individual ideas to the team, we were able to create a successful RGM that achieved our goal of feeding our dog. The project was well-received by our instructor and fellow classmates, which was a positive influence on the dynamics of the team. Our result was highly successful, even though we undertook this project as strangers. There was mutual respect and collaboration, and I believe my encouragement and support helped everyone feel included and empowered to contribute and be proud of our final product.
pfr: Throughout the project, I experienced a wide range of emotions such as excitement, frustration, and satisfaction. In the beginning, I was extremely excited and filled with anticipation about the possibility of meeting new people and I looked forward to the building a RGM together. However, as we began to brainstorm ideas, I started to feel frustrated due to the lack of progress and seeing that other teams were coming up with similar ideas to us. It was challenging to settle on one idea that was unique compared to other groups and interesting. I realized the importance of creativity when solving this problem. After a lot of brainstorming, we finally settled on the idea of feeding our dog using an RGM. But as we continued to think outside the box and came up with new ideas we slowly began to work better as a group as we understood our communication styles. For example, I realised my role in being a confident and encouraging peer who empowers more shy people to speak up and be heard in team discussion. In the end, I felt satisfied because I realised that even though at some points during our project timeline, there may be parts where we are discouraged, but by persevering and experimenting with different ideas, there will be innovative solution that I am proud of contributing to.
learning: Throughout the development of our RGM, I learnt several valuable lessons. Firstly, I learned the importance of patience and persistence when working on a team project, as it takes time and effort to come up with an innovative idea, and it is crucial to remain patient and not give up easily. Secondly, I realized the significance of effective communication skills in a team setting. Without clear communication, it can be challenging to coordinate efforts and make progress on the project. Going forward, I will prioritize improving my communication skills to be more effective in team projects. This means establishing deadlines for each person’s task earlier in the term and communicating with my tutor about any members who are not responding to the team’s messages. Finally, I realized that being encouraging is crucial in a team environment, and this determines the success of a project. We had to work together to design and build the RGM and our team avoided major disagreements and setbacks because we spoke to each other with kindness and respect and listened carefully to what we each had to say to ensure there was no confusion during communications. This streamlined the progression of our project. Without encouragement and kindness, there would not have been a collaborative environment. This is something I will take into future group projects. In conclusion, the experience of working on the group assignment taught me valuable lessons about creativity, communication, and teamwork. Going forward, I will work on improving my creativity, communication skills, and prioritizing teamwork to be more effective in group projects.

situation: For unit ENGG1050, the focus on the group project regarding the Rube Goldberg Model is a step-by-step process in which where the team’s progress is summarised in the weekly workshop through a 10-minute slideshow presentation. As a high-school graduate, I have been provided prior opportunities in preparing PowerPoint presentations and have adequate experience in making announcements in Year 12 class. However, the professional aspects involved in oral presentations are hugely different at Macquarie University. Expectations are high as the convenor for the workshop meeting has pointed out that speech as well as slide orientation needs to be concise and have a content structure. The concern regarding time constraints is strict as it is understood that real-life company meetings are not designed to suit the employee’s comfort. Students are trained to be flexible regardless of any interruption faced during a slideshow. For Week 11, it was my turn to present for Team A12. From certain feedback, I understood that the importance of visual representation is just as important as the content in each slide. For example, in one slide, a table format was displayed to show the before and after improvements that were made on RGM event reliability. Two different colours were assigned to separate the content before and after. Although the content was well-organised, the colour coordination was chosen poorly as the green-orange mix caused reading difficulty. Colour coordination comes naturally to a creative person. I find that I am lacking in this aspect as over the semester, my teammates have suggested other alternative methods to modify my RGM events to pass the reliability test threshold. As an aspiring engineering student, the quality to come up with original ideas is just as important as following your superior’s order. It defines capability to a certain extent.
task_action: There are dreamers, and then there are the realists. Both need each other to accomplish greater things in life. Back in Yr9, a poster needed to be designed for the WWII Holocaust. In a two-person group, one person is asked to type up the relevant content while the other had arrange the theme and images for the poster. The problem arose when almost all of the poster was composed of information. From this, I have understood the need for balance when compiling the 10 RGM events for Team A12. One member had his event ending with a water balloon being popped and the spilt water being collected in a bucket. To transition to the next event, a similar bucket element is required to zoom out of, but the member responsible for the said event has decided to change his focus from a pulley system to a projectile instead. Overall, the event order had to be re-arranged and this simple solution was suggested by a team member who got annoyed by a 20-minute quarrel that was wasted in zoom-meeting. The moral of this whole dilemma is that too much creative thinking can get on a realistic person’s last nerve.
result: For week 12, a group member who has avoided the role of the presenter was pointed out in Team A12’s group chat. Said person has eventually volunteered to make a slideshow but has clarified that it is not wise for him/her to speak as his words are not very fluent. The team has voted in favour that any marks denied from such an issue are not relevant to the tutors, but the speech needs to be shortened to meet the time limit of 10 minutes. The minute-taker assigned for week 12 was held responsible for timing the presenter’s speech duration. Through trial and error, 1600 words of content were shortened to 1180 to meet the requirement. In terms of the visual design of slides, a second opinion is advised by the Chairperson for Week 13 RGM Project Presentation.
pfr: Creativity is essential to bring out the originality centred around any tasks at hand. But it does not mean that others should prioritise the whims of one person to deny progression that is well established. Improvement is good, but it is a suggestion and not the only alternative sought after. Quick and efficient methods are just as valuable as a creative approach. If the end goal is to stand out and wow the audience, then might as well search out for RGM events in movie scenes. An oral presentation is most reliant on content, slides, and time constraint. Fluency is a hurdle that only makes it hard for the audience to understand what is being said. For that, practice is the only medicine. Accents can be mimicked with proper dedication.
learning: It is hard to accept rejection when a great idea is put aside for project completion. But if it irks that person so much, then bear the burden of taking on more responsibilities. Show that you are serious and are willing to go the extra mile for your selfishness in a group assignment. To quote Taylor Swift; “Haters gonna hate, shake it off!”
