To simplify the decision process, we created a lookup table that mapped out which gesture beats another, reducing the complexity of nested conditionals in our code. Next, we divided the coding tasks among the team members, assigning specific functions to individuals based on their strengths. For example, one member focused on user input validation while another worked on the game loop and scoring mechanism. I was responsible for integrating the different functions and ensuring they worked cohesively. This involved writing test cases for each function and debugging any issues during integration. After the initial development phase, we conducted extensive testing individually and as a group to identify and fix bugs. This included testing edge cases and unexpected inputs to ensure the program's robustness.
result: Our collective efforts culminated in the creation of a fully functional Rock, Paper, Scissors, Lizard, and Spock game that not only met all the project requirements but also showcased our team's prowess. The game logic was clear and efficient, allowing for smooth gameplay. We handled user inputs gracefully and determined game outcomes accurately, enhancing the overall user experience. This project yielded several positive outcomes. We not only completed the project within the given timeline but also presented a well-documented and thoroughly tested program. Our clear division of tasks and regular communication ensured effective teamwork, allowing us to collectively learn from each other's strengths and overcome challenges. Our professor commended our structured approach, particularly the effective use of the STAR framework, which bolstered our confidence in our problem-solving abilities. situation: Every week, our team must present to our tutor what we have completed so far in the week as a team. This mostly details an oral presentation of our team's Miro board contributions to the current week's tasks. This is done through a Zoom meeting, where the presenter shares their Miro board to the common room. This includes the group tutor and the other team's under that Tutor's charge.
task_action: We usually aim to finish our group discussions roughly 30 minutes before we are asked to return to the common room (where are asked to present). Usually I, along with the team, discuss the various ideas and options we have presented in our Miro board before deciding what to add/ remove from our board before presenting. We also go back and forth on the ideas on our board that truly reflect the spirit of the team, and whether or not we are confident in presenting this information to our tutor and the other groups. With this extra 30 minutes or so of time, I try to familiarise myself with the board's content and any diagrams/ infographics the team has come up with so that I may be able to better explain and preview it to the tutor and other groups. Once I am confident that I understand the content of the board well enough, I go ahead and structure it in a way that is easy for the other teams to follow along. This usually includes adding some sort of structure to annotations, adding colour and pictures to any boring words and having the Miro board appear presentable and clean before I give my oral presentation to the class. Upon presenting our team's board to the tutor, I try my best to talk slowly and clearly into my microphone so that everyone is able to keep up with my words and with the content being displayed. When talking, I also scroll across the Miro board to reference the content I'm explaining so that the audience is not forced to look for it. Due to bandwidth limitation in Zoom, the share screen stream is usually blurry. To compensate for this, I zoom into the Miro board so that it is legible enough for everyone to view. I also keep track of the time on my phone so that I know when to stop presenting and to wrap up before time is over.
result: Following these guidelines when it comes to presentation, I'm confident that our oral presentations every week are one of the best among our tutor's group. Taking that extra half an hour or so of time to properly go over the Miro board content and organizing it really helps me out during presentations.
pfr: The first 2 weeks of presenting were definitely the toughest to do. Obviously having university classes on Zoom is new to most people, including myself, so our team was not sure what to expect. Coupled with the fact that half our team was missing in the first week, we had a hard time presenting in the first week. Our content was all over the place, it wasn't complete and only half of our team contributed to it. I don't really remember a time where I had to present so abruptly on the spot with minimal preparation and in a much different environment and situation. In the past I'd have been notified ahead of time that I would be giving an oral presentation. This would leave me with ample time and space to collate my ideas and to process them in the most optimal form. But I'm glad I had such a shock that first week because I developed the skill to think quickly on my feet. This let me develop my aforementioned process of synthesising information and being able to quickly formulate an oral presentation over an online video call, which is something very new to me and many other students.
learning: By developing my oral presentation skills over Zoom video calls, this actually taught me a skill I never thought I needed: Improvisation and Quick Thinking. As I have alluded to before in the past, I'd usually be given ample time and space to think my presentation over, memorise my words and their delivery and any quippy or funny joke I have saved in my stash. But being told to present over Zoom, with little to no preparation, and to present to such a large audience meant that I had to adapt, and fast. Even though I agree our first two weeks of presentations weren't my best efforts, I felt as though they were a key stepping stone for my development later in the unit where we have to (soon) present our RGM machine to our tutor.

topic: The design process phasing and approaches
situation: I had decided to include a Galton board within my section of the Rube Goldberg machine, however I did not have one on hand and had no prior experience with constructing one from scratch.
task_action: I was to build a Galton board from scratch using supplies I had lying around the house as to maximise sustainability of the project and avoid trips to the shops and unnecessarily buying materials. I needed to learn how to make a Galton board, and apply my learnings to construct a working Galton board. Action: I took to google image search to take inspiration from a range of Galton board designs available on the internet, taking note of what materials were used, what kind of ball was passed through them, how large the pins in the board were etc. After the initial research phase, I decided with another group member for the sake of continuity I would use a ping pong ball and I took to the garage to find a scrap piece of wood that could act as the main basis of the construction of my Galton board as well as some pin-like objects that I could use in the construction of my board. I settled upon some nails and initially used a pencil and measurements of the ping pong balls diameter to mark out where I would hammer the nails into the board, I then tested the board with my pre measured points, however due to the thickness of the nails and my inaccuracy with a hammer, the gaps were far too small for the ball to fit through. I spent a day in the garage with an extra piece of scrap wood experimenting with different nail distances until I was able to test run the ball through the Galton board smoothly, allowing it to pass each row of nails either between two nails, or between one nail and the edge of the board.
result: As a result of my research and development, I was able to go from not having a Galton board and not knowing anything about how to construct one, to having a perfectly working Galton board, made out of recycled materials, ready for use in my section of the Rube Goldberg Machine.
pfr: Initially I was quite intimidated by the task, as I had no previous experience with similar processes of research and development of something from scratch, however I was also confident in my abilities and knew family members whom I live with (younger brother - mechanic, and father - DIY guru), were able to offer me any help that I may have required. I did not need any help however and as I got into the rhythm of trial and error, and gained some precision with the hammer after my practice attempts, meaning I was able to attain the desirable result and a Galton board I am quite proud of.
learning: Through my approach to this problem, I was able to gain understanding of all of the things that need to go right to result in a working Galton board. I believe that the skills I gained are quite widely applicable to a range of other projects that include construction of something from scratch. I am now confident that I would be able to build another Galton board from scratch even with different dimensions to the one I built as I am aware of the problems that may be faced during construction and efficient workarounds.

situation: Upon enrolling in ENGG1050 I discovered that the entire unit was to be conducted online. Lectures, tutorials, individual and group work; all to take place in an online environment. The unit runs this way to help us (the students) prepare to navigate the professional world, which is increasingly turning to online forums for communication. This means that there has been no face to face interaction with staff or students. As a result, we have had to employ a variety of strategies to facilitate communication between peers, particularly as this unit revolves around a group initiative to design and construct a Rube Goldberg Machine (RGM).
task_action: The task at hand has been to implement various streams of communication between myself and my group. The type of communication has to be professional and readily available to each individual to facilitate quick and easy transmission of information and ideas. We must ensure that all group members are on the same page at all times so that everyone is aware of their roles and responsibilities. ACTION: To communicate effectively amongst the group we have utilised many different online applications. These include Zoom, WhatsApp, Google Docs, and Miro. Each team meeting is held over Zoom and the agenda and minutes for the meetings are collaboratively created and shared via Google Docs. We organise the times for our meetings and pose questions/answers to each other outside of meeting times through a WhatsApp group chat. Miro has been used to create our team charter and timeline, to brainstorm, and to upload diagrams and sketches of our design solutions.
result: As a result of using numerous communication streams, my group has been able to successfully share our thoughts and ideas in a professional and constructive manner to progress the creation of our RGM. Zoom facilitates real time conversations, which are crucial in addressing and overcoming issues. For example, we ran into a problem regarding how each section of the machine would fit together. Using Zoom, we were able to conduct a quick survey of common materials each team member had access to in order to create the illusion of a seamless RGM. Creating and circulating our agendas and minutes via Google Docs has allowed group members to stay up to date with the team’s progress and to be aware of their responsibilities, even when unable to attend team meetings. WhatsApp has been crucial for sharing videos of the advancements made to the RGM. This enables the group to visualise how the RGM is going to look. It is very important to know how the section before your own looks, in order to match the lighting, background, and camera angle, and as a result, create a smooth transition. Finally, using Miro has allowed our group to have a visual record of the progression of our ideas. We are able to upload evolving designs and annotate each other’s work, demonstrating how Miro has been a highly useful mode of communication.
pfr: When I learned that the unit only ran online I felt concerned about how I would effectively communicate with my teachers and my peers. This concern was amplified when I discovered the majority of the unit focused on group work. I felt anxious that I wouldn’t be able to do well in this unit as I anticipated it to be very difficult to communicate with my group and complete work to a high standard while working online. I am very driven to succeed so the idea that I would not be collaborating with my group members in person made me feel that I wouldn’t be able to rely on my peers, in turn adding a lot of stress to my life.
learning: After taking part in ENGG1050 for the last 6 weeks, I have learned about the ease of working online. There are many different applications available that facilitate online collaboration, and in some cases make it preferable to physical meetings. For example, Miro has allowed us to upload images of our changing designs to a shared forum. This serves as visual evidence of the evolution of our RGM all in one place. While hard copies are important in their own right, they can not be easily accessed by other people. Miro has allowed me to work on my section of the machine outside of meeting hours, because I know I can always view the most up to date versions of the sections before and after me. Now that I know how beneficial it can be to work online, I will not be so hesitant to do so in the future. I will be more open to collaboration in virtual spaces, and will know that I can rely on individuals even when I have never met them. Looking forward, I will embrace online opportunities and think critically about how they can sometimes offer more than physical interactions.

situation: First of all, I want to share a quote from one of my favourite books, "The Creative Act: A Way of Being" by Rick Rubin. I didn't win, but I got a lot of positive feedback from the judges and other competitors. They noticed my work stood out because we were all supposed to show off our skills on DJ decks and mix music, but I took a different route. Instead of playing the usual tunes people expect, I decided to blend Mongolian sounds with electronic music, which turned out pretty cool. Now, some might think this has nothing to do with my engineering classes. But to me, DJing is a form of art, just like music and engineering are. They're all about creating something new and expressive.
task_action: So, the idea might be simple at first, something maybe a lot of us have thought about "mixing traditional folk songs with modern music". But actually bringing that idea to life, making it real, that was the real challenge for me. Like Rick Rubin points out in his book, "Creativity is like a dance between chaos and order". It's something we all understand, but I'm not saying it's impossible, actually making it happen is not that easy. So, what I did was listen to hundreds of Mongolian traditional songs and sounds that could blend with electronic music. Then came the real test: blending them together using DJ controllers, which was pretty good and unique according to my judges and competitors. DJ decks can get pretty complex with all the different controls and options, kind of like engineers working on big projects like bridges, etc. Sure, building a bridge is a much bigger task, but what I want to say is both rely on creativity.
result: So, what I'm getting at is this creativity is all around us. We can't live without creativity or imagination. We need them to thrive and to keep improving things, whether it's in music, engineering, or anything else. Sometimes, what might seem small or insignificant to you could actually be something totally new and groundbreaking for the world around us.

Not winning the Sydney competition stung a bit, but hearing compliments from my judges and others made it worth it. It proved for me that stepping outside of the box can land you in some pretty cool spots. This whole thing reminded me of my engineering classes. There, creativity isn't just about artistic stuff. it's all about solving problems in smart ways. Whether it's mixing tracks or building bridges, it's all about thinking outside the box.
learning: So, digging into my creative side really paid off, not just in music but it reminds me of our engineering projects, too. topic: Initiative and the willingness to make decisions in the face of uncertainty
situation: In Week 3 of our Rube Goldberg machine project, we reached a point where we needed to decide on a theme and define what our PROBLEM STATEMENT for our machine was actually going to be. Choosing the right theme/problem statement was crucial because it would shape everything we did afterwards, from the design to the final build. Everyone in the team had different ideas about what we should do, and each idea came with its own challenges and unknowns.
task_action: As one of the active members during the project planning phase, I took on the role of helping our team decide on a theme for our Rube Goldberg machine. This task meant dealing with a lot of different opinions and trying to find a common ground that worked for everyone. Our project had specific goals and limitations we needed to consider. ACTION: Understanding the importance of making a well-informed decision, I set up an extra meeting to help us get past our deadlock. At the meeting, I laid out a SWOT analysis for each theme idea, looking at the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats. I had prepared this by asking everyone for their input beforehand. This approach gave us a clear framework to discuss each option. I encouraged everyone to share their thoughts and stressed the importance of choosing a theme that was not only creative but also practical, considering what we could actually achieve with the resources and time we had.
result: After a lot of discussion and a clear look at the pros and cons of each theme, we all agreed on one that was both creative and doable within our limits and the time we had. This decision brought us all together with a clear direction, really shaping how we planned and carried out the rest of our project. Everyone valued the organized way we made our decision, which not only solved the issue at hand but also made us stronger as a team for future projects. This whole experience really highlighted how important it is to step up and make decisions, even when things aren’t certain, and it helped me grow a lot in leading and bringing people together.
pfr: The weight of leading the decision-making felt huge, I was really excited but also a bit nervous. But as we got into the meeting and I started sharing the SWOT analysis, things started to click. Breaking the decision into smaller, clear parts made it less intimidating and helped everyone, including me, feel more secure in our choices.
learning: I've really seen the value of taking charge and using structured methods like SWOT to guide decisions, especially when things feel uncertain. It didn’t just help us choose wisely, it made sure everyone felt part of the process. situation: * Recently, I went Scuba Diving as a type 1 diabetic. This was not my first time diving with diabetes, and at the beginning of the dive I gave a small presentation about this. I talked about what it meant to dive as a diabetic, including the potential risks and what I would need from people in case a situation arises. However, during the dive a complication arose due to my diabetes. The group I was diving with felt confused and unprepared, they were unsure of what they should do. This made me realise something, that I didn’t do an adequate job informing people of their role to play in case of an emergency. I needed to prepare and script a better presentation, to explain my diabetes to my dive partners.
task_action: * A close friend of mine is one of the best cave divers in the world. He put me in touch with one of his students, another type 1 diabetic. We sat on a phone call for about 4 hours, brainstorming all of the potential problems I could have underwater due to my diabetes and what those problems would mean for me, for the people I’m diving with, and how those problems would be managed or mitigated. Once we came up with that list, we worked out which of those problems I could manage on my own, and which of those problems required help from other people. From there, we created clear and concise explanations, including props and images, to explain only the problems that would require help from other people.
result: * We came up with a new presentation, one which did a much better job of preparing people. We did this by explaining the condition, what it means for me as a diver, the important hand symbol for diving with diabetes and what it means for a dive, the potential things I need from people, and stressing that certain problems just need time for me to work through them on my own, and that if I require assistance I will signal people for it. Using this method, I was able to create a much more effective presentation. I tried this out recently and did a mock simulation of a diabetes problem underwater, and no one from the diving group was confused or felt unequipped to handle this situation. This presentation was a success.
pfr: * Initially, the whole ordeal of creating a new presentation was daunting. Not just because I had to communicate important information, but also because I had to answer some very uncomfortable questions about myself. I realised to avoid answering these questions I had been incredibly conservative with my first message, alluding too but not explicitly stating the problems that could be caused and the consequences of those problems. To fix this, I had to be very honest with myself about what would occur if these problems did occur and weren’t treated promptly and efficiently, and that is that I would die. I had to answer these questions, not just for my sake but for my diving group’s sake as well. By working out what each problem was, how it could be managed or mitigated, and whether I would need help (and if so what kind of help) to solve each problem, was instrumental in creating a new presentation. The phone call I had with a good friend who is also a diabetic diver proved instrumental in solving this issue.
learning: * What I learnt throughout this whole ordeal is something about myself, that I have a tendency to sugar coat things and make them easier to understand or hear. I saw first-hand the problems that can arise from this, and how being honest and forward with most definitely the optimal approach. It saves time, effort and causes less problems overall. I also learnt how valuable discussion and a brainstorming session can be, especially with someone who knows a topic as well as you. I don’t often look for help with my diabetes, but discussing problem areas with another diabetic scuba diver proved instrumental in identifying problems I hadn’t even considered. In the end, I realized how important testing and practice are after simulating a presentation and encountering a scenario with a different group of divers, which helped me see areas that needed clearer explanation. Through this encounter, I realised the crucial significance of honesty and openness in a professional setting, while also understanding the importance of relying on others.

topic: Perseverance, urgency and will to deliver, resourcefulness and flexibility
situation: In the third week of this semester, I was given a substantial assignment that was due in week 7. Initially, I did not prioritise it because the due date was so far away. By week 5 I had only completed about 15% of the work. I became overwhelmed with other pressing assignments and placed this one on the backburner, even as the due date rapidly approached.
task_action: As week 6 arrived and the assignment was due the next week, I realised I needed to make this my top priority. I began chipping away at the work, determined not to submit it late and incur a 5% penalty. The assignment was much larger than I had anticipated, requiring extensive research and writing for each of the 10 questions, ultimately taking around 2hr per question. To manage the workload, I made significant sacrifices, staying up late and working through the Easter long weekend to make progress. I had to cancel some of my mid-week plans in week 7 to focus solely on completing this large assignment. On the day before the due date, I was on campus and found myself preemptively completing class work to allow me to go home early work on the remaining sections at home.
result: Through sheer perseverance, urgency, and a strong will to deliver, I was able to complete the entire 6000-word assignment by 12:55am, submitting it with just 4 minutes to spare. This required a high degree of resourcefulness and flexibility, as I had to adapt my schedule and priorities to ensure I could devote the necessary time and effort to this assignment. Whilst the experience was extremely stressful, the outcome was successful. I was able to submit the assignment on time without incurring any late penalties. This experience has taught me valuable lessons about planning, organisation, and the importance of not becoming complacent when faced with a daunting task. In the future, I will aim to better assess the scope of an assignment and allocate my time accordingly, rather than leaving it until the last minute.
pfr: Looking back on this experience, I feel a range of emotions. I'm proud that I was able to persevere and ultimately complete the assignment on time, despite the significant challenges and obstacles I faced. The sheer determination and willpower required to push through and successfully complete the assignment is something I can take pride in. However, I also feel a sense of frustration with myself for not managing my time and priorities better from the get go. The fact that I allowed myself to become so overwhelmed and behind on such a substantial assignment is a bit embarrassing considering I normally am so on top of things like this. I shouldn't have let it get to the point where I was sacrificing other commitments and staying up late every night just to get it done. At the time, I was under immense stress and anxiety. The pressure of that looming deadline and the fear of failing to submit on time weighed heavily on me as I have never submitted late before. There were moments where I considered just leaving it until tomorrow and accepting the 5% penalty. That level of stress and uncertainty is not something I enjoy going through. The feeling of relief after submitting the assignment and knowing that it was over was something that I did thoroughly enjoy, but it did not outweigh the stress experienced to get there. Overall, this experience has been a valuable learning opportunity, though a difficult one. I've gained some important insights about myself and how I approach challenging academic tasks. While I’ve shown myself that I display the ability to persevere and that I have an underlying sense of urgency to get tasks done, it's clear to me that I need to work on my time management and prioritisation skills.
learning: The most important lesson I learned from this experience is that proactive preparation and organisation are more important than my ability to manage and react to a crisis. Going forward, I will ensure to thoroughly examine any new tasks or assignments as soon as they are assigned, and devise a practical schedule and strategy. I will be sure to not underestimate or ignore the amount of work that is required for a task. Furthermore, I've come to understand the importance of discipline and perseverance in the face of major challenges. Even though I want to steer clear of these last-minute stressful situations in the future, I am confident that I possess the strength and resolve to persevere when necessary. The satisfaction of submitting that assignment on time, despite the difficulty, is proof of that. Also, I now recognise the importance of flexibility and adaptability. I had to quickly adapt and come up with new strategies to make up the time and mental space I needed to concentrate on the assignment when my initial activities and obligations had to be postponed or cancelled. Being able to easily adjust my schedule and priorities is a skill I hope to keep. All in all, this difficult experience has given me insightful knowledge that I will use moving ahead. I'm sure I can use these lessons to improve my organisation, initiative, and resilience as a student, making me more capable of managing the challenges I may face whilst studying.

situation: At home, my space is in the garage. I have my computer, my tools/materials, musical instruments and have carved out my own little space because our house is quite small and everyone is living on top of eachother. Because our house is quite small, the garage is also the primary storage location for my mum, her partner and my sister, and as people accumulate random items my space in the house is filled with other peoples mess, this is a source of conflict in our household.
task_action: A potential solution didn’t jump out at me naturally to resolve this storage issue/conflict, I was working on welding together a flatbar in the garage (an obstacle for skateboarding) and my back was hurting because I didn’t have a workbench for these types of activities and I had to bend over to work on the ground. When I stood up, back aching, it occurred to me that if I used the materials in the garage to build a workbench there would be more room to store peoples clutter on the shelves, I would be utilising the offcuts taking up room in the garage and I wouldn’t be hurting my back every time I wanted to undertake a personal project. So I put my half finished flatbar aside and spoke to my family to see what they would think of my idea, and they liked it! I finished the workbench in the following days and then went on to build a few shelves in the garage with leftover materials.
result: Upon completion I was so excited. My space, the garage, was clean and I had much more room to move around, I also have a sense of pride everytime I use the workbench to build something, knowing that my work has helped me with undertaking future projects is very satisfying. Unfortunately, others in the house have seen all the new space I’ve carved out and it seems the garage is slowly starting to fill up with junk again (although its still currently far better than it was).
pfr: The garage space being tidier than before – as silly as it may sound - has bought me a lot of joy and pride because this is a space that I use almost everyday. I don’t always go out of my way to correct minor issues in life, being aware of these pain points isn’t something that comes naturally to me. Since I’ve put in so much time to creating this space and making it tidy, I get quite defensive of others trying to dump their unused items in the garage and feel it is a slap in the face if my family do this. I know they aren’t doing it to intentionally annoy me, so I should try not to take these actions personally.
learning: When it comes to addressing pain points, one take away from this scenario is that it shouldn’t take multiple issues stacking up and being seemingly unbearable to take action. The fact that I felt such a sense of pride to have improved the situation in my space is a testimony, looking out for these issues so that they can be addressed can really improve your daily living. I see some friends and family who seem to really have their life quite organised, I think of my grandad who has small things like hooks to hold wires out of the way and their lives do seem to run a whole lot more smoothly when addressing minor pain points like this regularly. This only occurs through constantly looking out for pain points, and brainstorming/acting on solutions. It may seem like an uninspired lesson to take from the conflict regarding others dumping rubbish in my space, but I’m aware that in coming years when I move out of home, having ample space to store equipment/items is something I’m now looking out for! situation: Leading up to the end of the ENGG3050 unit, it has come to my attention that ethics, integrity, and social responsibility are incredibly important in the engineering field. Both from my own personal experiences, as well as research done for my presentations done in class, it is clear that ethics and integrity have grown in the field and is changing vastly. This comes along with new technologies such as Artificial Intelligence models like ChatGPT as well as looking at renewable energies and technologies related to the company I presented in week 10, Wallbox. Ensuring as an engineer we understand our social responsibilities and how we take technology to the next level will ensure a positive impact is made on the society around us and improve the lives of future generations.
task_action: In terms of artificial intelligence, it can be applied to so many tasks which have occurred throughout my engineering degree. Especially in tasks which require writing like many lab reports or even these reflections, I have seen people using ChatGPT to copy and paste answers. I dislike this, and it does not reflect my true intentions as an engineer. Of course it is easy to do and would reduce the time it would take to do assessments, but it does not deliver the same gratitude and understanding that actually being involved in those assignments brings. This issue has been raised by many of the higher ups and academics at Macquarie University where they have addressed the issue of plagiarised and artificially created content, which I agree with. It should be used as a learning tool and to provide background information as needed, like google that gives summarised information. In extreme cases, it is important to hold moral ethics and integrity as an engineer as anything we create and present to the public will be used by people maybe across the world, so ensuring we take some level of social responsibility during our careers is important, and artificial intelligence does not have the capacity to think and consider the consequences and the many challenges that come with engineering. topic: Trade-offs, judgment, and balance in resolution
situation: This semester, I overloaded myself by taking five units instead of the usual four. This resulted in periods where I was overwhelmed by an immense amount of work and assignments. For one of my units, we were assigned a significant Continuous Professional Development (CPD) project worth 60% of the final grade. Around weeks 5 or 6, I finalised my CPD project idea, choosing to work on a facial expression recognition program. Initially, I underestimated the project's complexity, thinking it wouldn't be too challenging since I had some prior exposure to machine learning. However, I made the mistake of prioritising other assignments and exam preparation over the holidays, completely neglecting my CPD project until week 9.
task_action: When I realised I needed to start working on the CPD immediately, panic set in. As I began, I quickly understood that learning everything and coding a complete model or program alone within the limited time frame was unrealistic. I used my better judgement and made the strategic decision to prioritise learning and comprehending the topics over focusing solely on delivering a final product. I slowed my pace, created a plan, and concentrated on grasping the concepts and expanding my knowledge rather than stressing over producing a fully functional program. I also made sacrifices in my personal life, cancelling social plans and non-essential activities like going to the gym to dedicate time to this task.
result: These trade-offs and my re-prioritisation proved to be a wise decision. By week 11, I had gained significantly more knowledge and understanding than I would have if I had solely focused on creating a working program. I became well-versed in machine learning topics and developed an understanding of how to approach problems, even if I didn't have a final product to showcase. This approach reduced my stress and equipped me with the theoretical knowledge needed to eventually start coding a functional product to present to the class. This experience taught me valuable lessons about acknowledging the importance of tasks, prioritising them accordingly, and managing my time more effectively. I realised that I should have recognised the significance of the CPD project earlier and prioritised it over other assignments. Furthermore, I became aware of my tendency to work on one assignment at a time, hoping to complete it quickly, which often led to a backlog of assignments due simultaneously. I recognised the need to change this approach to avoid overwhelming stress when facing multiple deadlines.
pfr: Looking back and reflecting on this experience evokes a range of emotions. On one hand, I feel a sense of pride and accomplishment for persevering through the challenges, gaining a deeper understanding of machine learning and working on a functional program. The determination and resilience required to navigate this situation successfully is something I can take pride in. However, I also feel frustrated with myself for not managing my time and priorities more effectively from the get go. The fact that I allowed the situation to escalate to a point where I was overwhelmed and behind on such a significant assignment is a source of embarrassment, as I typically pride myself on being organised and proactive. I’m quite disappointed that I ended up in a situation that required trade-offs in the first place. Deciding to prioritise learning and understanding the concepts over delivering a final product was a difficult but necessary decision. It required me to sacrifice personal time and activities, such as socialising and going to the gym, to dedicate myself fully to the task at hand. Although challenging, this approach allowed me to reduce stress and gain a deeper understanding of the subject matter. Throughout the process, I had to exercise my judgement and find a balance between my academic responsibilities and personal life. It was a constant struggle to manage my time effectively and avoid the tendency to work on assignments sequentially, which often led to overwhelming backlogs. Looking back, I can appreciate the valuable learning opportunity this experience provided, albeit a challenging one. It has allowed me to gain important insights about myself and how I approach demanding academic tasks.
learning: This experience taught me invaluable lessons about time management, prioritisation, and making well-informed trade-offs to achieve a balanced outcome. I realised the importance of acknowledging the significance of tasks early on and allocating my time and efforts accordingly. Moving forward, I will strive to change my approach to completing assignments. Instead of focusing on one task at a time, I will work on multiple assignments simultaneously to ensure steady progress across the board. This proactive approach will help me avoid overwhelming situations and manage my workload more effectively. Furthermore, I have learned the value of exercising my judgement and making strategic trade-offs when faced with competing priorities. While it may be challenging to sacrifice personal time or activities, it is sometimes necessary to ensure academic success and maintain a healthy balance. This experience has also highlighted the importance of self-reflection and continuous learning. By reflecting on my actions and their consequences, I have gained insights that will undoubtedly shape my future decision-making processes and help me navigate similar situations more effectively.

The decision to use an agile approach allowed for the task to be broken down and tackled one step at a time with continual improvements reducing the workload and stress of the task. I was able to quickly and easily iterate on the designs addressing the issues of the components as they became apparent saving time in theorising and ensuring a more reliable mechanism.
learning: Using an Agile approach to design allows for higher productivity and effectiveness in designing systems with many variables and interacting elements. The approach encourages iteration on design making it easy to follow and ensures reliability as bad or inefficient designs are quickly resolved or discounted. Through this experience, I have come to a new level of appreciation and understanding for the different development approaches and their use cases, especially with the agile approach when designing intricate systems.

situation: I encountered a significant pain point related to the inconsistency in task display on the learning platform used for course management. This issue was negatively impacting both instructors and students, leading to confusion, missed deadlines, and decreased efficiency in academic activities.
task_action: To address this pain point, I took the initiative to devise potential solutions independently. Recognising the importance of offering suggestions to improve the learning platform, my task was to brainstorm and propose measures to enhance the consistency of task display. Firstly, I conducted research to understand the root causes of the problem and identify potential solutions. I reviewed literature on user experience design, online learning platforms, and best practices in course management systems to inform my approach. Based on my research, I generated a list of potential solutions to improve task display consistency on the learning platform. These included: 1. Developing standardised templates for course instructors to use when creating tasks, ensuring uniformity in presentation across all courses. 2. Implementing automated checks and validations to identify and rectify inconsistencies in task display, such as missing deadlines or incomplete instructions. 3. Introducing a feedback mechanism for students to report issues with task display, enabling quick resolution by course administrators. 4. Providing training sessions and resources for faculty members on effective course design practices and utilising the learning platform's features to ensure consistent task display. I organised my suggestions in a structured manner, outlining the benefits and feasibility of each proposed solution. I also considered potential challenges and limitations, as well as the resources and support required for implementation.
result: By independently suggesting potential solutions to improve task display consistency on the learning platform, I contributed to raising awareness of the issue and initiating discussions on possible remedies. While the solutions were not implemented, my suggestions could serve as a starting point for further exploration and action by relevant stakeholders. Additionally, my proactive approach demonstrated initiative and problem-solving skills, highlighting my commitment to enhancing the learning experience for both instructors and students.

Furthermore, I recognise the value of preparation and planning in effectively extracting information from others. By taking the time to research effective interviewing techniques and develop a list of structured questions, I can mitigate the challenges associated with formulating enquiries on the spot. Additionally, I will seek support and guidance from mentors or peers who may offer valuable advice on communication strategies and overcoming shyness. Overall, this experience has served as a learning opportunity for personal growth and development. By confronting my fears and honing my communication skills, I can become more effective at gathering insights and addressing challenges in future endeavours.

situation: In my previous course, ENGG2000/3000, students were allocated to a specific group within a team depending on their specialization (three groups: Structures, Motions, and Communications). As a mechanical student, I was placed in the ‘Structures’ group with four other civil/mechanical students. In my structures group, there were two students in their third year, and I was in my second year. The roles and responsibilities of each group were unique and specific to their discipline. The ‘Structures’ group was responsible for cube structure design, selection of material, and finally, manufacturing and assembly processes. The ‘Communications’ group was responsible for the software elements such as programming and debugging. The ‘Motions’ group was responsible for the motor plus sensor selection and electrical connections (wiring). Progress videos and pictures of the marble cube were compiled in a final video presentation.
task_action: As the structures group we brainstormed, and the finalized design concepts formulated for the structural element of the marble cube. Further, our group identified the relevant materials required for each relevant subsystem. Next, we gathered all the necessary materials and tools to build each section. Also, as one of the requirements is materials from certain suppliers only, this meant that if we did not have the materials or equipment available at these suppliers, we would look for alternatives by substituting them with something similar. Parts of the finalized design were slightly changed to adequately meet the supplier's requirements. Once each section was constructed, the group would perform 20 test runs and record the success rate. Next, the source of errors was identified for each subsystem and suggested improvements were amended to the system. Improvements or adjustments were made with the assistance of the other two groups in the team. Then, another 20 test runs were performed, and the improved success rate was documented. Additionally, a collection of videos and pictures were taken to document progress. Simultaneously, both other groups (communications and motions) were in frequent communication with our group, using our feedback, to make their selection of motors or sensors and their relevant programming. Whenever any changes big or small need to be made to the speed of the motors or the rate of the sensors, one member from the other group would make the necessary adjustments. Also, any other issue such as an increase or decrease in power output or dimension of the motor or sensor would be amended with the help of the other groups in the team. This streamlined the process as roadblocks or delays were attended to promptly.
result: By the end of the semester, we had developed a fully functioning marvellous marble machine that performed all the requirements outlined by our client. Also, the initial success rate and section reliability were improved and adjusted as necessary with the assistance of the other two groups. Immediate communication with the other groups when any issue presented itself allowed for efficient reliability improvements of the marble cube. Further, the progress videos and pictures were edited into the video presentation.
pfr: Initially, I felt that we were not competent to take on this project as it was a relatively substantial task given the client's requirements. I thought that it required a greater level of technical skills which we did not have to complete this project given the time constraints. During the mid-term break, our structures group (most of whom were available to make it in person to the workshop) began the optimization process by testing each subsystem and improving the reliability of the marble machine with the assistance of members from other groups. I felt that we would face too many overwhelming issues regarding the hardware and software limitations which would impede the progress of the marble cube. Luckily, we managed to address the issues in the marble cube promptly due to the competent members of our communications and motions group. The other members were very responsive and experienced in their areas which allowed our collective team to progress as rapidly as it did. Without their relevant knowledge and skills, I don’t believe we would have met the deadlines.
learning: Through this, it was evident that many members with different roles and responsibilities were necessary to complete a substantial project such as the marble cube. By having the relevant technical groups such as structures, communications, and motions with their assigned task, it meant that there was no confusion in how the cube workload was distributed. Further, it allowed for the rapid rate of design, development, and testing as multiple members were working on various parts of the marble cube at any given moment. Any mistakes or oversights were rectified or added promptly. Also, massive projects require knowledge and expertise that is wide-ranging and expansive, so having members from different technical backgrounds who have been assigned certain roles and responsibilities allows for immediate workload allocation. As a result, each member became more collaborative and communicative in the process which would help them in their career development as an engineer. Hence, having a clear understanding of the roles and responsibilities of each member of a team allows for an efficient and effective strategy to complete a massive project.

situation: Throughout this semester, I have been working with the Australian Glass & Window Association in a technical administration role where I am responsible for auditing glass & window thermal performance simulations submitted to the Window Energy and Rating Scheme (WERS). I am responsible for ensuring that simulations made in LBNL software: Therm, Window and Optics, are simulated in accordance to rules and regulations set by the AFRC (Australian Fenestration Registration Council) and the NFRC (National Fenestration Registration Council) through the analysis of cross-sectional models of window frame members and their relevant thermal behaviour. This year has brought a significant spike in the submission count for simulations, and has created a backlog of pending submissions that must be audited. This has created some urgency to work through submissions as quickly as possible to maintain a low submission count without sacrificing thoroughness and consistency.
task_action: My primary task was to increase my auditing efficiency for these thermal simulations without sacrificing the thoroughness that ensures all simulations are consistent. I began by optimising my auditing processes through the use of more adequate file management methods to make keeping track of my completed audits and quickly switching between different submissions much faster. I adjusted visual settings that made keeping track of my cursor and identifying errors easier, further increasing audit speed. I followed this with increasing the amount of communication between the Engineers I work with and myself, clarifying issues that I am uncertain on with them rather than taking the time to read through the large list of rules and standards. This allowed for me to reduce time wasted finding specific rules through making use of the resources around me to quickly refer to points in my relevant documents and their advice. This also assisted with increasing my understanding of the rules, reducing the amount I need to refer to any documents. I also began tracking my progress more thoroughly which went hand-in-hand with my file management processes, allowing myself and the Engineers I work with to update association members on wait times and create plans to manage progress through the backlog.
result: Through implementation of the above actions, I aimed to address the increased workload that came with the increased submissions effectively, ensuring that my auditing processes remained robust, efficient and in full compliance with all relevant standards.
pfr: When I first heard about the expected spike in submission counts, I felt a relatively significant amount of pressure. I am an auditor to relieve the workload relating to WERS off my Engineer co-workers. The urgency related to processing these submissions without sacrificing accuracy created a unique circumstance, as speed and thoroughness were critical to maintaining a good workload for all parties. Upon reflecting on these initial feelings, I have realised that my stress was primarily due to the fear of failing to prove that I am a good worker. I realised in the moment that although cutting corners to reduce the backlog was an easy option, it would impact my integrity, and it was my responsibility to ensure that I optimise my processes in order to show that I am thorough and that all products on the WERS database are accurate and correct. As I began developing my actions to address this issue, I grew more confidence as I received positive feedback regarding my accuracy and efficiency, which led to more confidence and in turn, more efficiency. This realisation was crucial in handling the situation correctly.
learning: From this experience, I have learned the importance of maintaining integrity as an Engineer, regardless of the pressures of timelines and good image. I learnt that handling issues in a constructive way is much more valuable than cutting corners. Continuous improvement in processes is essential with changing demands, complimenting this with greater communication skills allow for efficiency without sacrificing essential responsibilities Engineers have. Through these reflections, I have developed a better understanding of the importance relating to responsibility in Engineering. This experience has been extremely enlightening in the benefits of streamlining approaches without sacrificing quality.

They are critical to achieving a good result within the subject and test on a wide variety of skills including not only technical problem solving but also presentational and articulation-based skills.

With this knowledge as my foundation, I proceeded to brainstorm potential solutions, considering various factors such as software, hardware, administration, humanistic approaches, and innovative hybrid models, as discussed in lectures. I felt uncertain at times about the suitability of my solutions across the different categories. Delving deeper, I explored how the integration of AI could address related pain points such as research, marking, and feedback processes. To tackle this challenge, I really had to remind myself of why I am here to study and push through to be able to sit down, find the mental capacity to learn and apply what I had left to get it done and give it my best to ensure I had to regrets after. When I encountered obstacles, such as my arduino not working, and software glitches, I had to be resourceful and adapt. I met up with some friends and while they were working on their code or other projects, I was able to borrow those to test what I had done to try and understand what the next step could be. Throughout this period, I made a point to share my experiences with my sister, emphasizing the importance of perseverance and resourcefulness in the face of academic challenges. I encouraged her to stay focused on her goals and to be willing to adapt her strategies when necessary. Although her and I approach things very differently, sharing those pathways can still help provide an alternative perspective.

The support and resources I gained through my resourcefulness and flexibility, such as working alongside friends and borrowing their equipment, were crucial in maintaining my momentum.
learning: This experience reinforced the importance of perseverance, urgency, resourcefulness, and flexibility in the face of adversity. I learned that even when faced with significant personal and academic challenges, staying focused on the end goal and breaking it down into smaller, achievable steps can make all the difference. I discovered the value of leaning on my support network and being proactive in seeking out the resources I needed to succeed. Moving forward, I will apply these lessons to future challenges, both in my studies and personal life. I will continue to share my experiences with my sister, encouraging her to cultivate these qualities and to learn from both my successes and mistakes. This experience has strengthened my belief that we can overcome even the most trying circumstances and deliver on our commitments while staying true to our values and goals. Regardless of what the circumstances are or the level or pressure, to be able to keep pushing through, being able to be relaxed and plan the approach rather than just diving in can help you achieve whatever it is you're trying to and this is definitely a skill that can be applied in all aspects of my life and one I plan on developing further moving forward.

Following that, I sketched a rough state machine diagram to help me conceptualize my code structure and determine my approach to the final result. Unfortunately, I got sick during that week, lacking behind on the plan. I believed that I would be able to pull it off, but I wasn't seeing it through; I didn't see myself fixing the bugs in my code for a long time. I divided the burden of other assignments and the Minor project for the last week into hours and days. I prioritized the assignments based in their due dates. Therefore, completing all other assignments, I resumed coding the countdown timer. I sat goals and measurable achievements to help track my progress, but I was falling behind. We were allowed to use generative AI, so I used it to help speed my progress. Even after using AI, I had to manually fix the inaccuracies of the code.
result: After long hours, I was able to complete 8/9 tests and submitted the code half hour before the due time. The code worked perfectly other than the integration of a potentiometer to change the brightness of the 7-segment display.

The pressure of meeting the deadline and managing other assignments further intensified these feelings. Regardless, I was super determined, and just couldn't give up on planning according to the changing situation. At the end, I was partially satisfied with my project as I wasn't able to finish the last test but was also relieved that it was finally over.
learning: The most important thing that I learned from this experience of mine was the power of perseverance. Moreover, being resourceful helps incredibly. The use of generative AI was an effective way of speeding up the progress, as it helped in fixing bugs and understanding C language. Lastly, flexibility in an engineer is a must, because that determines his skills in changing circumstances and how he performs under pressure.

task_action: A digital list of checks that had been compiled earlier and made into an online form was gone-through by pairs of workers and items ticked off one at a time. Several changes had been made to the form so that tasks specific to one boat or another could be marked as "not applicable" on forms related to boats that did not have the related equipment. Unfortunately, some undocumented changes had been made to the form by members of the operations or software departments without the knowledge of the shop workers or shop management. These forms are initially stored and filled-out client-side.and are only updated on the server when the form is submitted. Software or coding limitations meant that forms could not be submitted until completely filled out.
result: Some of the undocumented changes, along with the limitations of the form software, IT infrastructure and form design meant that forms could not be completed and filled out for some boats, and checks had to be documented manually in the old-fashioned way after being transcribed from a half-completed form. This resulted in significant confusion and wasted some of everyone's time, including workers and management from both the workshop and other departments. Luckily the launch of the boats was not delayed, but it added potential risk of a no-go to an already fraught situation.
pfr: I feel that the use of online forms is an ingenious way of ensuring consistent and instantaneous distribution of information regarding the check status of vessels within the company. However, its implementation both technically and within the communication infrastructure of the company leaves something to be desired. The issues arise from a combination of ambiguity as to the accountability of individuals for certain tasks and a lack of conscious effort to incorporate the forms and their continual updating into the existing communication infrastructure of the company. For example, the individuals filling out the forms are personally accountable for performing the checks and must sign their names on the form. This is a good thing, and ensures that if something goes wrong, the team knows who to ask about the state of the equipment before the incident in order to determine if the failure was a technical one or a failure of procedure allowing human error to be introduced. This responsibility does not appear to extend to the people who are directly making the form webpage, who have no direct contact with the boats. This means changes are made to the form that may betray slight misunderstandings or lack of understanding about the systems aboard the vessels, and which make the forms impossible to fill out completely and submit, causing delays. In addition, nobody initially knows who made the changes and on whose instruction they were made, so it is additionally difficult to rectify the problem. I feel more could be done to improve the fitness-for-purpose of the form software used for pre-operation checks, to facilitate better communication between those making the forms and those filling them out, and to extend personal accountability to those making changes to the forms so that changes may be documented and problems fixed more quickly.
learning: Several changes could be made to improve the pre-operation check form situation and reduce the likelihood of further issues. Firstly a very short meeting between workshop and software management to outline the issue and discuss possible fixes to the issues with submission and form editing would be helpful. Forms should be stored server-side and updated live as individual points are ticked. The "submission" button should be little more than a mark of completion that temporarily locks editing of the form. Secondly, a series of three or four short, half-hour meetings between the workshop manager and the lead programmer for the forms webpage should be arranged over the following week. This would allow the programmer time to visit the vessel and see the equipment for which he is adding form items and so that the workshop manager can help him arrive at a list and form structure that best reflects the needs of the workshop and operations teams. It would also allow the workshop manager to visit the programmer during his development process to collaborate and suggest changes to the form as it is being finalised. Similar meetings should be arranged in the week preceding the introduction of any significant changes to the form or its contents. Secondly, changes to the forms should be documented and numbered as with a more formal software development process. Updates should also be signed and dated. This would help ensure that any changes made are not simply ad-hoc additions made by the software team without checking with operations or the workshop and are instead made with purpose and following approval by management of all parties. Thirdly, a hard-copy backup for these forms should be devised so that in the event of a software issue, the checks can still be made and documented without immediate delay, to be transcribed into the digital archive later when time is not so short.

topic: The transferable skill I will be focusing on is transparency, accountability and collaboration in a team operation within the context of the Rube Goldberg Machine project.
situation: We as a team needed to start working on our individual Rube Goldberg Machine components.
task_action: We set a hard deadline for when we wanted all the machines and individual component videos to be completed (21st of October) and expected each team member to hold themselves accountable and deliver what was expected of them in a timely manner. We outlined a few expectations beforehand, such as that we wanted the videos to be filmed solely in landscape mode to make the final video more cohesive and that the footage should be relatively high quality. Members of the group also discussed with each other how they were planning on conducting the transitions between each element. For example, two members were using water bottles as a transition device, and had a conversation about what brand they were planning on using to make it as cohesive as possible. Throughout the week, team members sent videos of their machines into our group chat and uploaded them in the shared Google Drive for easier access. We also held team members who seemed to be lagging behind accountable by asking them where they were at with their machine and assessing to see if they needed any help by encouraging collaboration. Furthermore, we were all transparent with any issues we were having or any problems that could implicate the timely delivery of our components. For example, some team members had assessment tasks from other subjects that they were prioritizing which we all understood would take more leeway.
result: The result were 5 videos of every team member's two components that could be combined into a final video achieved through consistently holding people accountable.
pfr: It was initially an intimidating task for us as we were worried about being too assertive or too forthcoming when talking to team members and holding them accountable for not delivering work on time. For example, we have a team member who has not handed in any assessment task all semester and has barely contributed to the overall project. We weren't sure if he was going to actually produce a final video that we could use, so we held him accountable by reaching out to him and asking him where he was at and if he thought completing the project was feasible. He was transparent with us, and told us that he didn't think he could, but failed to provide a legitimate reason. We then communicated and collaborated with the team to remove him from the group as we didn't want to impede our own progress. Thus, we only had 5 RGM videos produced instead of the 6. But, we were able to exercise effective accountability over specific team members in a way that seemed reasonable.
learning: By consistently holding team members accountable throughout the process of developing our final video, we were able to learn how to be properly assertive, communicative and how to prioritize the team's best interest. It was important for us to be confrontational and transparent with how we all felt in regards to the lack of contribution from certain team members to move forward and be successful.

situation: Reflecting upon my time and resource management through this past semester, I notice that this had become a lacking skill of mine during the start of my study at Macquarie. So far I am in my second semester of studies at Macquarie, and whilst I believe I started my studies very excited and optimistic, university life has definitely given me a wakeup call. As since, beginning I’ve had to face many problems of varying types. Eventually through trial and error and help from my peers I have been able to solve these problems by, beginning to adjust my attitude and habits to further aid my future life as a student and eventually an engineer.
task_action: Undergoing attempts to improve my time and resource management, I have attempted to use several methods such as, to-do listing suggested by my ENG1050 tutor, prioritising tasks, improving my organisation, removing unnecessary distractions and improving my overall health. Thusly I have explored all of these options and created a subsequent approach to my time and resource management.
result: The approach I have now devised is to use to-do listing, prioritising tasks, removing unnecessary distractions and improving my overall health. By creating to-do listings, I am now able to layout all future tasks for each and the subsequent order in which I must complete each task, indirectly creating a prioritised order of tasks. Hence this is aided by removing unnecessary distractions from my workstation, by moving my workstation to a quieter room in the house and placing my mobile phone in a separate room whilst I am studying. Another addition is improving my overall health, lately I have been falling ill a lot due to unnecessary stress and not keeping a regular sleep schedule and/or not eating properly. I have now begun to prioritize improving these items, as pushing myself to the breaking point not healthy.

Hence during the break, I took time to reflect on this and I concluded that this was not a healthy or sustainable approach to my university life, and I need to take a more balanced approach to my studies. I believe reality has reflected these assumptions very well as during the first semester I got injured during rock climbing many times as I was not paying attention to my health properly and I became disconnected with my friends, but once I began implementing these changes, I noticed considerable improvements to my health and attitude. With this knowledge in my future studies, I plan to implement similar strategies to balance my life to excel in all aspects.
learning: Through these experiences I have learned that maintaining a balanced life is crucial as, this allows me to consistently apply myself at a balanced rate. I have also realised that to make sure study is effective there are certain protocols you can take in to create an effective study environment and avoid burnout. Hence by approaching my latest studies using a more balanced method with effective strategies, I have been able to have a much healthier approach to my university study. Now I am also able to enjoy my social life and continue climbing whilst still staying on top of all of my studies. Although one other aspect I have realised is that I must add some flexibility to this strategy as some unforeseen events can come and effect this approach severally.

topic: The transferable skills I will be reflecting on are “Test, verification, validation, and certification” and “The innovation process” and how these relate to the engineering process.
situation: Following up on the first 5 weeks of ENG1050, from week 6 to week 11 as part of team C15 we have had the massive task of innovating and validating our RGM design. As the next step in our design process, we had to finalise our preliminary designs and began constructing our RGM. We had to overcome reliability issues across all of our events implementing the “test, verification, validation, and certification” processes to finalise these events.
task_action: For the past few weeks we have been tasked with the small-scale testing, full scale testing and overall reliability improvements of each event. As one of the few teams doing the whole RGM as one machine, we have run into a lot of problems requiring a lot of testing, innovation and problem solving to improve and finalise our designs. As a group we had to meticulously plan and organise the materials we needed, the times we were meeting and how to set up the machine. Initially when setting up the RGM we ran into a lot of problems. We began testing the first and second events and realised that our small-scale reliabilities did not translate well to the full-scale testing. The led to a lot of innovation and changing of designs within the first few events and the rest of the RGM. With continuous changes made to every event it was crucial that we set up the events right as we only had one shot to get it right. Unlike the other teams who could take days/weeks to perfect their events we ran into time constrains which meant our events were not as perfect as I would have liked however I am pleased with what we got done and happy that the construction is finished.
result: For the first 2 events we had to improve the reliability of the golf ball rolling down a table and knocking into a pendulum. Our reliability was basically non-existent with the ball rolling off the table, bouncing unpredictably and not going where we needed it. We had to test just the first event about 20 or so times before we got it right. To verify and validate the reliability of the event we had to make some major improvements with the limited resources we had. We found using tape as a sort of springy barrier worked well to dampen the bouncing of the golf ball. The innovative thinking that we as a group had to come up with was rather difficult yet rewarding when it worked. We also decided to split up the events to make sure they would work seamlessly whilst not taking us hours to get that one perfect event. We also realised that it was taking us a very long time to set up each event, with our first meeting together, we successfully created and filmed 7 events over 6 hours in week 10. We then planned for another meeting the following week, in which we finalised our RGM filming.
pfr: In order to test and verify a design within a team requires a lot of dedication. I never realised how hard the reliability stages of the design would be to overcome. Through hours of testing in person I thought that we had finally got it, but when we fixed one thing, another broke. During this process though, as a team we learnt how to deal with these challenges, often all of us working on it was too much. We split into smaller teams, whilst one was innovating and improving the design on one event, the others were preparing and testing the next event. This help workflow of the team and finishing off the events within the time we had allocated over the few days we had to construct the RGM. Testing takes time, a lot of time, and to finally verify and validate that an event has worked was rewarding. However in choosing to make the RGM as one whole machine was a challenge, yes we overcame it but was it worth it in the end? There are positives and negatives to taking this approach: (+) It made us work together better as a team, coming up with new ideas, building on others’ ideas and being able to set it up together as a whole. As a whole team, it felt very united and something we could all be proud of. When one person was struggling to improve the event they were working on, someone would come up with an idea. This was then implemented and improved upon and eventually validified by it working a majority of the time. As a group it was very enjoyable and social environment, this helped keep motivation high when testing failed and pushing for innovation within the designs (-) There were often times we got distracted. One group may have finished their event and were waiting on the others to finish on their design. At times we genuinely got bored and began mucking around which wasn’t the best for the productivity for our team. Other times people would take over leaving others with nothing to do but watch. Sometimes people would make suggestions, but they were ignored and put down, and often just getting something thrown together and finished was more important than actually improving the design.
learning: Honestly I’ve learnt that the final product in this case is not the most crucial thing to take away from this unit. I was so worried about everything being perfect, all the events looking perfect and working seamlessly. It was so much more important to focus on the innovation and creativity, with coming up with solutions to problems, which is at the heart of engineering itself. I thought having the most amazing filming angles and finished product would be all we were aiming for, but this isn’t the aspirations of the rest of the group. I found that not everyone will have the same end goal as me, but to work together and push each other was something that was inspiring. Throughout the last few weeks we have done extensive testing and reflecting on how we are improving and advancing in our designs, which has been an eye opening and rewarding experience. Again, much like what I reflected during the first 5 weeks, a lot of the seemingly easy steps throughout this designing, reliability and construction phase turned out to be quite difficult to navigate. It’s hard to swallow my pride and accept that not everyone is aiming for high marks with this unit, and that they just want to get this project done and over with. I hope that in some way I have convinced the others in my group to push themselves in the testing, validating and innovation of our machine, but in the end I’m happy with the friends that I’ve made during this unit and how much I’ve learnt throughout the engineering process and it relates to my future goals and career.

situation: During weeks one through eleven of ENGG1050, I was assigned to a group and instructed to work together to design, build, test, and record a functioning Rube Goldberg Machine (RGM). task_action: We began brainstorming ideas for a theme we could have for our RGM and originally decided on the theme of making a birthday cake. We continued to make our weekly presentations and create our RGM over the holiday. We presented our documented testing results on reliability and our new iterations to our tutor group. Finally, we had our final designs of our RGM and are now about to soon submit our final video.

pfr: I have found that throughout this project, the online nature of the class has caused time and resource management to be slightly more difficult to determine. In the beginning, when deciding on a theme, we went too big in our idea and over-allocated time and resources that we, as university students, do not have. I personally as President of the Macquarie Machining Society am very busy, trying to balance school, running a society, and social life, in addition to trying to be conscious of my health by making sure to sleep enough and eat well. We as a group just underestimated how much a project of that scale would take timewise to execute, let alone the resources of space and materials to test the reliability of the cake-making RGM. Thankfully, under the advisement of our tutor, we were guided to scale back the size of our RGM to smaller sections, while still trying to keep to the overall theme of using a cake in a fun way. Another way the online nature of the course has been challenging in time management has been in creating the presentations. Being online has made it hard to contact people and arrange for them to do work both inside and outside of class. Oftentimes we will create a Google Slides presentation, however, will not fill in the content until late in the evening the night before we present. Finally, the online nature of the course creates the challenge of group members turning off their cameras which makes it difficult to assign tasks as you do not know whether or not the member is at the computer. However, they do often attend in person meetings where they are more willing to help contribute to tasks assigned.
learning: By setting realistic goals and allocating resources efficiently, a project of this scale is very easy to accomplish and can be an enjoyable experience. However, when deadlines are not enforced it demotivates and does not hold people accountable, thereby creating stress and poor results, such as overtime presentations due to miscommunication over the content.
