So each group member would choose 2-3 events under a chosen theme (colour, environmentally safe, etc.) for their part in the RGM. We acknowledge that each group member has their strengths and weaknesses, so for the building process, the more experienced group members will be assigned the more difficult series, and the least experienced will be given series that they have the home resources to complete that aren't as difficult. To balance out workload, the group members would be given the task of reviewing the RGM and looking for ways to improve it, so as to be more efficient with time.
result: The outcome of following the task plan and measuring time realistically was being able to have a complete detailed design of our specific RGM. Each group member has a solid foundational idea on how their series is going to result and a list of necessary materials for each series, which was discussed during the brainstorm process.
pfr: Beforehand the task of methodically creating an RGM was overwhelming for me and all the other members of group A7. From past group experiences I knew about how coming together as a group and managing time would affect our final design, and prior experience has resulted in scope-creep, multitasking, lack of communication and stress, all stemming from having no time management.

We approached this issue by holding each member accountable for the work they were given to complete (we agreed to have 2 or more people working on the same part as to promote communication and accountability as the group member they were assigned with would make sure that they contributed). situation: This semester in ENGG3050, we were asked to research a startup and create a 4 minute presentation on a specific aspect of the company. This work was to be completed in groups of 5, and team members would need to collaborate in order to form cohesive presentations that flow on from each other. An extensive list of startups was provided to choose from, and group members could be chosen from students present in class. Specific research topics would be on a particular aspect of the startup's business operations and entrepreneurial journey, adhering to the Business Model Canvas components. The 5 research topics included: management structure and people/company culture, funding process and general business case, growth strategy and scaling journey, market opportunity and technical edge, and customer segment and product placement.
task_action: After forming groups, research would need to be undertaken to learn more about the startup and create a presentation relevant to the chosen company. We were encouraged to select a startup in an industry or market sector that interested us, to make researching the company more engaging and generate more enthusiasm during the presentation. After choosing a startup within the group, specific aspects of the startup would be selected by each member to conduct detailed research on. Prior to week 9, when the first member of our group would be presenting, my group planned to meet in-person and conduct research on the startup together, to allow for better collaboration and to encourage each other in our work. General research on the company would first be undertaken, to gain an understanding of who the startup is and what they do on the whole. In conducting this research, insight into the company's global expansion and inter-continental reach would be completed to develop an understanding of the importance of global perspectives and interactions. For some, companies, their geographic location or language may prevent them from expanding into new markets or making connections with overseas suppliers, manufacturers and customers. It is important to consider the global presence and the social, political and environmental landscape of a company, particularly when the company is from an area the researcher is unfamiliar with, considering standards and practices may be drastically different to that of Australia. ACTION: In my group, we selected to research and present on the EV charging and energy solutions startup Wallbox, which was founded in 2015 by two ex-tesla employees in Barcelona, Spain. After group deliberation, we decided that I would present on Topic D - Market Opportunity and Technological Edge. In researching Wallbox, I learned about how they progressed from presenting their prototype at startup pitch competitions to gain exposure and funds to making partnerships with international manufacturing chains to aid in their supply chains on a global scale. In the span of a decade, Wallbox progressed from a startup of two engineers, to a company with over 500 employees, 1 million customers worldwide and a valuation of $320 million. After gaining funding through winning a startup competition in 2016, angel investors in the late 2010s and 5 rounds of Series A VC funding in 2020, Wallbox was able to produce their first product for distribution within Spain. I found it interesting to learn about the large extent of the funding required to support the creation of an MVP and production, even though it was still limited to within the company's founding country at this stage. Wallbox initially had difficulty expanding their products into global markets, as company employees had little experience with overseas markets and foreign supply chains. Furthermore, the language barrier prevented CEO's Enric and Eduard from comfortably contacting potential business partners and investors. The somewhat turbulent political landscape in Spain combined with the lack of local manufacturers meant Wallbox had to look for alternative ways of designing and manufacturing their product. To overcome the language barrier and challenges imposed by the region the startup was founded in, Wallbox made the decision to hire employees overseas with better knowledge of the local area, to help assist them in global manufacturing and distribution. Knowing China's importance in global manufacturing given its ability to produce products on a large scale at low prices, Wallbox entered into a partnership with Changchun FAWSN, to become a key player in EV charger manufacturing in the region. The challenges faced by Wallbox in expanding into international markets reflects their inexperience and lack of knowledge of the global landscape.
result: In researching Wallbox and their experiences with global manufacturing and trade, I gained a greater insight into the global considerations and experiences that need to be taken into account when making business deals or considering international partnerships. While it's easy to assume that all humans, or in this instance CEOs and business owners, have similar views and experiences to that of yourself, however this simply isn't true. Each individual is uniquely shaped by the environment they live in and their life experiences. How people choose to respond to these often negative life experiences is what shapes them as a person. Similarly, companies are moulded by the industry they operate in, their country of origin and the business decisions made by those in charge of the company. Particularly when considering countries other than Australia, the living conditions, political stability, civil status and environmental landscape can influence company experiences and culture. In researching Spanish startup Wallbox, I have learned about the factors that come into play when making decisions on a global scale and how differences in opinion and experience can be resultant of unique environments within a particular country. This experience has helped me develop a global perspective and understanding of the unique circumstances that shape individuals and businesses on an international scale.
pfr: In researching my chosen company Wallbox, I felt intrigued by the business decisions made and the circumstances that informed their decision making at the time. After struggling to secure funding, Wallbox branched out of their comfort zone to secure partnerships with a Chinese manufacturing company, despite the geographical and language barriers. The CEOs of Wallbox themselves expressed their hesitation with the business move, as they had no idea what to expect. However, Wallbox chose to embrace the partnership, and within a year, the two companies had become synonymous, with Wallbox expressing their profound gratitude for the Chinese company. The positive experience Wallbox had encouraged them to expand further into Asian EV markets and even start new partnerships with countries in other continents, including North America, Africa, Oceana and Europe. In 2018, Wallbox underwent a culture shift when looking to expand beyond the Spanish market and venture in to new areas. Instead of relying on hard data and quantitative information, Wallbox took into consideration the qualitative aspects of potential partnerships with new regions, and saw the benefit of incorporating the unique ideas and perspectives of individuals from other countries into their workforce and target market. This shift from relying on knowledge-based concepts for business direction to considering mindset-based improvements and perspectives allowed the company to expand into new territories with great success. Researching and understanding Wallbox's progression from a small Spanish startup working out of a one room warehouse to a global powerhouse in EV charging production with customers in 80 countries has been intriguing, informative and impactful. Their experience has allowed me to see the merit in considering how a situation or problem impacts not just myself, but also how the scenario relates to people around the world.
learning: Researching and learning about the experience of Wallbox has taught me the importance of considering the impact of ones surroundings and environment on who they are, whether it be a person, or a large company. On a global scale, the majority of people have different life experiences to myself and have been moulded by a combination of factors including the political landscape, unique experiences, the environment and leadership schemes. It's crucial to never judge a person (or company for that matter) on face value and instead take the time to understand why something is the way that it is. I have also learned the importance of respecting the opinions and views of diverse countries, cultures, heritages, ages and lifestyles. Collaborating with individuals and entities substantially different to yourself can be extremely beneficial as they bring unique perspectives and opinions to a situation that can help improve a design or situation. For example, Wallbox had limited knowledge of the Asian EV market, however collaboration with Chinese manufacturing company Changchun FAWSN helped them gain insights into the Chinese EV landscape to better understand what consumers would be expecting of them. This helped Wallbox to develop a viable product for the EV market that met the unique charging, time and location parameters of global customers. Wallbox's experiences have helped me to develop a global perspective, and consider the impact situations may have on others, depending on their personal experiences and the environment in which they operate. Adjusting the lens through which I see the world around me will help me better empathise with people and understand where they are coming from when their opinions, ideas and experiences may differ to my own. I have learned to consider the complex nature of people and companies, whilst considering the different viewpoints that guide their decision making, the cultural perspectives that shape their experiences and the global extent to which issues may impact others around the world.

situation: During my Second year at university, I participated in a group project for our engineering course. Our assignment was to design a 200mm cube that allowed marbles to travel through a series of interconnected events. A conflict arose between our team and the Structures team regarding a critical component needed to achieve a high distinction. This disagreement risked delaying the project and creating lasting tension between the teams, potentially jeopardizing our collaborative efforts and project success.
task_action: My responsibility was to mediate between the two teams to find a compromise that would enable us to stay on schedule and meet the expectations of both the Motions and Structures teams. I needed to facilitate a solution that would keep the project moving forward without sacrificing the integrity of the final product. Spin-offs: I discussed the possibility of creating a subsidiary focused solely on the new technology. 4. topic: The most prominent transferable skill that has stood out within my group is reflecting over is ACCOUNTABILITY IN A TEAM'S OPERATION.
situation: As a team, we needed to ensure that each individual commits and follows through with weekly activities and finishes delegated tasks on time.
task_action: In our very first meeting as a team, we designed a team charter that describes and outlines the responsibilities and goals that we agree upon in undertaking the projects and assessments in this unit. We ensured and evaluated the alignment of expectations such as satisfactory levels of work, meeting times and communication channels, were established and to remain consistent in meeting those requirements in our group. Our team applied the S.M.A.R.T.E.R (Specific, Meaningful, Achievable, Relevant, Time-Bound, Evaluate and Re-adjust) framework to clearly define our project goals, roles and other commitments and have a verbal and written agreement to abide by these rules we have set for ourselves.
result: After the first team activities, there were some team members that did not abide by the charter and as a team made a few re-adjustments. After those re-adjustments were made, team members complied with their required tasks and were held accountable in team activities and assessable tasks.
pfr: As we set the first amendment of our team charter, I was hesitant about the motivation and commitments my other peers may contribute to the group project. By assessing their communication and general behaviour, I had some doubts. Thankfully, after the first team activities, re-adjustments could be made as early as possible to avoid situations where individual team members were unable to commit and were not held accountable when committing to a task. The framework we used as a group enabled us to adapt to these issues in a swift manner and make the necessary changes to how we go about confronting the accountability of each team member. I am grateful that the majority of my team is flexible in addressing the individual shortcomings of others and can commit to the end goal that we all agreed upon during our first meeting.
learning: Working with strict set rules may not always work in an ever-changing environment and may dissuade members to have less initiative, motivation, and general enjoyment of a team’s operation. Our team approach our measures of accountability by being flexible with the commitments of each individual member whilst maintaining certain thresholds of criteria that need to be met during assessable tasks. As the majority of our team has worked well thus far with a strong team dynamic, there is always room to improve in ensuring that our team is held accountable to the goals and roles we have set ourselves from day one. This is something I have seen that always recurs in both academic and commercial settings in the workplace. The ability to adapt is key to our team's accountability in team operations.

topic:
Team member management. 

Managing members of a team who are not meeting expectations and how to work with them to achieve that outcome that best serves everyone.
situation: We had a team member who has been continuously lacking in their contribution and effort throughout the semester.
task_action: Our task for this particular issue was to identify why this team member wasn't contributing to the level that was expected, as there are many reasons as to why this could be happening. Such as them not feeling that their contribution was appreciated, they didn't 'fit in' with the group, or other personal reasons that could be happening in their life. After some discussion within the rest of the team, we decided a good course of action was to message the team member and let them know that the rest of the group was unhappy with their performance. This felt like the right thing to do as the underperformer may not have even know that they weren't contributing enough. The message was important also in that it created evidence for us as a team that we had reached out and started to try and manage the situation. This could be important in future to show our teachers, in case our submitted work was lacking due to the performance of the problem member.
result: We received responses from the member, in which they apologised, and we hoped this would improve the situation going forward. At first we thought their contribution was starting to improve, however, within two week of sending the message it has become clear that their contribution is highly unlikely to improve. The team and I are now in discussions on how to manage this, with the lacking team member's RGM components likely to be excluded(if they ever get made) and their place in the final presentation to be taken by another member.
pfr: My feelings towards this situation were that of disappointment, as to have one member failing to contribute amongst what is otherwise a well functioning team, really hindered our team cohesion and constantly inhibited any planning or structure we made as a team. This disappointment led to me feeling frustrated, as over the semester there just seemed to be no effort made by the underperforming member to take part in even the bare minimum - yet they were quick to apologise and act remorseful when it was brought up. It felt very 'all talk no action', as they would agree to complete parts of group work, yet never came through and whenever placed in a position where their knowledge was tested, they failed miserably. Finally, I have to say that I felt sorry for this person, as I don't know what's happening in their life and the reasons for their performance. It bodes ill for the rest of their engineering education if they fail to perform in a 1000 level course.
learning: By talking as a team and hearing different perspectives on the position we had been placed in, we were able to put together a level headed approach that took all people into consideration. I admit to being lacking in compassion at times, and the input of my other team members helped me see the issue from sides I wouldn't have considered if left to making the decision on my own. Through this, I was able to not only learn effective team management skills, but also the importance of emotional consideration when dealing with other people.

task_action: During week 8, we reacquainted and chatted about what we did over the break, this established a more friendly atmosphere in the meeting. Following this I took initiative and addressed the shortcoming of our leisure, we were behind and thus we brainstormed ways to remedy this issue, by constructing and improving our components during the meeting, during construction we had meaningful conversations and multitasked our way back on track. During week 9, the team faced the dilemma of presenting our improvements to the ‘Group C Possie’, a majority of the team hadn’t yet implemented their improvements, thus I took the initiative to present my improvements, this way I could ensure that the presenter knew the intricacies of the implemented improvements and thus is able to answer any questions the audience may have. This willingness to volunteer myself, enabled me to remove the weight over the team, as my team placed their trust in my ability to present, and this motivation cleared the uncertainties I had. In my opinion this led to the best presentation our group has delivered.
result: The outcome of the initiative I took, led to the smooth operation of the following weeks goals and objectives, and with the teams help I am able to confidently make decisions, knowing my team will back me up the entire way. This strengthened the unity of our group and grew each members confidence in taking the initiative to solve group dilemmas.
pfr: From my perspective, when our group reunited after the break, I felt that a vast majority of the momentum/enthusiasm was lost, and this created a similar experience to the first week our group met, it was uncomfortable, thus I broke the ice, I queried how everyone’s break was, this willingness to persevere my feelings worked, and I felt like we were part of a team again. I addressed how we hadn’t constructed any of our components yet and what we needed to do going forward. Thus we collaborated and constructed for the remainder of that period. learning: This team-based project has truly taught me the importance of initiating conversations, as you cannot expect every meeting to go smoothly, and without an initiator this project would have far more challenges further down the line, as communication is the key to group projects. topic:
A skill that I have developed throughout this course has been the skill and technique of looking at solutions and determining if it is a realistic solution. I believe this skill is important for engineers to help save on time and resources.

Throughout the development of the RGM project there have been many solutions developed, each with different and unique concepts. While many of these solutions were interesting, I was quick to point out that many of them were not possible due to a variety of factors such as time, complexity, and cost. After some team discussion it was decided that we would use more simple solutions to ensure that the project was completed on time.

Critical thinking is vitally important to engineers throughout all stages of the project. Looking at solutions objectively and with an open mind helps ensure that solutions can be created within the give time frame and budget. While it is important to understand when a solution is achievable, it is just as important to know when a solution is not.
situation: We needed to review our solutions to our RGM, which involves boiling an egg.
task_action: Look at the solutions objectively in our weekly meetings; listing the pros and cons for each solution; understanding the complexity and time it would take to complete the solution.
result: Many solutions to our RGM were created that the team and I believe are achievable within the given time frame and budget
pfr: It was fun to brainstorm different ideas for each event of the RGM. However, it was quite disheartening telling some of my team members that their solutions and ideas would be hard to achieve and complete due to time and complexity. While they didn't hold any grudges against me and were happy that I pointed out some issues with their ideas, it still bears some weight on my shoulders as I feel like I might have limited their creativity. However, after speaking with some other teams about their progress throughout this project and how they have faced challenges and issues with the complexity and budget of their events, I am confident that I made the right decision to point out some of the issues involved with our original solutions
learning: Coming up with effective solutions is essential for an engineer. However, it is arguably more important to be able to identify issues and challenges when coming up with new solutions. This can help save time, money, and ensure that the product that you are developing is completed in an above satisfactory way.

situation: We needed to develop creative ways to develop our rube Goldberg machine so it maintains a practical function of switching off an alarm clock, but also make it creative enough so it is interesting to watch from the viewers perspective.
task_action: After discussion with the team members, using the zoom breakout rooms, phone conversations and text conversations, it was understood that rube Goldberg machines function on the 6 simple machines; pulleys, levers, inclined planes, wheel and axle, wedges and screws. This information was then included onto a Miro board so we could brainstorm creative solutions involving these machines. For example, wheel and axles can be accomplished via use of a toy car, which uses the wheel and axles to roll down another simple machine, an inclined plane. Once we had brainstormed possible solutions, we then determined which ones would be possible to create with the equipment limitations of each member. In this way we would be able to dedicate time and resources to the creative solutions we can produce, instead of having to apply effort or purchasing resources to solutions we can't accomplish.
result: The result is the ability for each team member to successfully be able to accomplish a certain solution towards the project using the materials they have, without the need to purchase any items. These solutions will involve the application of the 6 simple machines and therefore be both entertaining to view, while also being true to the essence of what a rube Goldberg machine is.
pfr: When conducting projects such as this, occasionally ambition can get the better of one or all members of the team, myself included. This is where one or all of the team members produce ideas that are unreasonable or impossible to achieve in the given time frame. This prompts project creep as the more time dedicated to these overly complicated creative designs, the less time spent on the completion of the whole project. In our rube Goldberg machine we have avoided this effect and instead chosen less complex, but still creative, solutions to the project.
learning: From knowing the temptation to create overly ambitious solutions to projects, which ultimately result in the incompletion of tasks and the project whole, I have attempted a new strategy by prioritising the whole project over just a few specific parts. This is a learning experience due to projects I have done in the past where I choose tasks that would be above and beyond, however due to time and materials constraints, they aren't realistically achievable. Through the experience of this unit and prior events, I have also realised the importance of working and presenting ideas as a team. My colleagues produce ideas of themselves, and provide constructive criticism on ideas to ensure we all agree on creative, but attainable solutions that are ideal to complete our project.

topic: ENGG1050 has allowed my team to improve our oral presentation skills through the weekly presentations in preparation for both the final Rube Goldberg Machine presentation and when we need to demonstrate our employability for a future job. Through modifying ideas seen from other groups and adapting to the feedback received, we have been able to create the best presentations possible. We saw how important communicating through oral presentations is as it is the way people share ideas with others and influence their decisions. Our goal was to achieve 100% in our weekly presentation marks and, later on, score highly in our final presentation.
situation: Every week, starting in Week 2, our teams have had to give a weekly presentation to the other teams in our Tutor group. If chosen, we would then present to our Posse. This presentation is based on the work completed throughout the week prior and the previous workshop to demonstrate how our Rube Goldberg Machine is progressing and what we are learning from it.
task_action: We needed to come up with a presentation based on each week’s topic, centering around what stage in our Rube Goldberg Machine we were up to by rotating through our team, ensuring that everyone had a turn. It is a collaborative task for everyone to work on before the chosen person presents during the Friday workshop, using the feedback we are given from our tutor on the previous presentation/s. Some of this feedback was a major aspect of the presentation that many teams were struggling with. When presenting the information, it had to be useful and relevant without cramming too much in one screen so that the audience wouldn’t know where to look. In order to create the best presentation possible, we used our time to provide the presenter with various graphs, tables or other visual aids to make the presentation look aesthetically pleasing and informative. We also worked together on providing a basic outline of what needed to be conveyed in the presentation to make the job of creating it easier for the presenter. To ensure the time stayed below five minutes, the presenter practiced beforehand, cutting or modifying sections as best they could while also seeking advice from other team members. Although these tasks were actioned correctly in most weeks, one week there was miscommunication within the group and each team member thought another person was presenting.
result: In the latter situation, everyone thought they were not the presenter which resulted in an awkward silence as we each waited for someone to present. However, since we hadn’t planned for this, nothing happened and we soon realised the mistake after texting in our group chat to find out what had happened. This meant that one team member had to step up and he presented an off the cuff highlight of what we had been doing in the past week. Despite this hiccup, after executing our ideas to improve our presentations and using careful planning, we finally reached our goal and received 100% for our last presentation.
pfr: At first, we were all still getting to know each other and didn’t know how to proactively collaborate on a presentation. Our very first presentation, in Week 2, was presented by me and I had felt very lost due to not having anything to base my presentation off of and little to no help from my equally confused team members. Fortunately, through doing this every week, we were able to gather the necessary ideas and structure to implement in creating a better presentation. We found that using a PowerPoint slideshow was a better method of maintaining control over the presentation and keeping the audience in one place at a time than scrolling rather aimlessly through our Miro boards. This positively aided our teamwork as we began to work together on the plan for each week at our weekly meetings which boosted our team morale and brought us closer together. For me personally, I gained more confidence in my presenting and oral skills, and was able to produce a great presentation with my team’s help to get us the marks we wanted.
learning: I learnt a good many new skills in oral presentation which I can use, both in university and in any future career as it is an incredibly easily transferable skill. My team learnt how to communicate by sending multiple reminders and making sure everyone is on the same page so that we don’t have a repeat of our presentation disaster and ensure that someone will be presenting that week. We also learnt collaboration is crucial so that each team member understands everything, such as the equations used or an explanation of an event, which means that we can all answer relevant questions and know how to best explain it to other people without leaving a team member behind. While those skills in the backend of oral presentations are important, we also gained skills that are more visible to the audience. These include the best methods of getting the necessary information across (such as using graphs and only certain sections of tables instead of the whole thing), keeping under a time limit (by practicing and anticipating any mishaps while still leaving time for questions) and staying engaging throughout the presentation (by keeping it professional in a formal way while also including an occasional joke to draw the audience in). These aspects came together to make the package of what I have learnt, both individually and with my team, when it comes to the skill of oral presentation.

learning: Keeping a balance between tenacity and adaptability is one of the most important lessons I took away from this experience. topic: IDENTIFYING THE ISSUE, PROBLEM, OR PARADOX
situation: We needed to increase our Rube Goldberg Machine reliability as a whole. In doing so we need to identify the issues and problems we were having with each individual component to devise a way to resolve it.
task_action: To determine the issues we used brainstorming sessions and root cause analysis as a group to determine the possible issues that we were having. This allowed us to understand what issues and problems were arising as we all discussed what they might be and also possible solutions to resolve them. To do this we asked these questions; what happened, why did it happen, what can we do to fix it. Which formed the bases of our root cause analysis.
result: The results of this root cause analysis allowed us to increase the reliability of our Rube Goldberg Machine greatly. This can be seen with our reliability increasing from 4% to 52% reliable. This process also allowed us to as a group understand each component in greater detail and share ideas on how to resolve the issue of each machine as often the issue we determined to be most affecting the components was a simple one that was overlooked.
pfr: The process of identifying the issues and problems with our Rube Goldberg Machine was a difficult task as we as a group designed and planned each component and when it didn't work as expected it took us a substantial amount of time to determine what the issues with our designs could be. Although as we watched the videos of each other's designs and discussed what was happening we soon realized what the issues were. Often finding why it was happening was again fairly difficult. Not to mention working out how to fix the issues. Although at the end of this process when we worked out the issues and then actually fixed them it was a quite joyful moment as we were able to see that our ideas were actually effective.
learning: Through this experience of determining the issues and problems in our Rube Goldberg Machine. We learnt how to as a group undertake root cause analysis and how humbling it can be after planning and building something that there are so many issues that need addressing. We also learnt that working as a group and having fresh eyes on the problems allowed us to determine what was actually causing it and often it was a small thing that we overlooked causing the issue. situation: We had to begin constructing the action events of our RGM’s.
task_action: In preparation for week 8’s workshop we were asked to create a presentation on our RGM components individual reliabilities. Consequently, we were required to begin construction of the RGM events. We aimed to distribute the events equally amongst group members in our pre-workshop meeting. In this meeting, we created a Miro board with each unique action event and the materials required in each component. Action events were subsequently split between members based on who possessed necessary materials for a particular component. For example, I had string required for the zipline event and I had the cloth for our tablecloth event, and therefore I was assigned these two events. Following this meeting, each member was given the responsibility to construct and test their event, approximately 10-20 times, to determine reliability and then fill in their events subsection in our presentation for week 8. By the time of this workshop, we had tested a total of 6 events. I had tested the zipline event, however not extensively due to time restraints, and I could not acquire the slinky required in the tablecloth event, hence failing to test it. We presented these 6 events and their individual reliabilities in the week 8 workshop. The following week 9’s presentation required us to improve upon the individual reliability of our events, subsequently requiring us to construct what we failed to construct in the previous week. A pre-meeting was conducted where we discussed our failed attempt to get all action events in the previous week’s presentation, with a prevailing issue being time management, and thus decided on how to move forward. Specifically, we agreed each team member should allocate time to construct and test the remaining action events at least 2 days prior to our week 9 workshop. This deadline was put in place so that if someone had still not completed their event, they could ask for assistance in completing their event. Furthermore, we discussed each component we had already completed and how to improve reliability, with members suggesting changes in materials and alternative approaches to increase successful attempts. In order to improve time management each member decided and set aside 2 hours on a certain day to complete their assignments.

These assumptions were based of factors such as Available resources and complexity of the idea.

In addition, after our successful brainstorming session, as a group, the events were evaluated based on their complexity and availability from resources. topic: Perseverance, urgency and will to deliver, resourcefulness and flexibility
situation: The goal of building a Rube Goldberg machine to fill a cup with water was the focus of our ENGG1050 course project. It needed careful preparation and execution. About halfway through the project's duration, a big obstacle presented itself to our crew. Our first design's intricacy was proving to be a barrier, endangering not only the machine's dependability but also our chance to meet the deadline. This insight made it imperative to reevaluate and modify the plan.
task_action: In light of the circumstances, our team decided to convene a number of brainstorming meetings with the goal of streamlining our design without sacrificing the innovative spirit of the project. We understood that each member brought distinct perspectives and abilities to the table, and that it was critical to capitalize on this diversity in order to execute a successful pivot. As part of the action plan, each team member had to critically assess the parts of the machine that they had been allocated, with the aim of determining where possible simplifications may be made. The creation of a buddy system, which pairs team members to offer criticism and ideas for improvement on each other's work, was implemented to support this effort. I organised regular team meetings to ensure that everyone was clear on their tasks and able to share the latest research findings. To gain a more comprehensive understanding of the market, we also engaged local consultants and partners to help us understand the economic forces and cultural differences in a given region. I led the team in a SWOT analysis (i.e. Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities and Threats analysis) and developed a series of scenario plans for entry strategies.

These charts helped us identify potential opportunities and risks, and developed a detailed market entry plan for us. situation: During my third year in the mechanical engineering program, our team was tasked with designing a new gearbox using CREO. The project required us to design the gearbox and all the components using CREO, present all the relevant calculations to all the class in regards to the components, manufacture the gearbox and test its functionality. This project was part of our course in the unit mechanical design, and it involved applying both theoretical knowledge and practical skills. Our team consisted of three members, each with different strengths.
task_action: As the project leader, my primary responsibility was to ensure that our team collaborated effectively and met all project deadlines. This involved coordinating the efforts of each team member, managing resources, and addressing any conflicts or challenges that arose during the project. Additionally, I needed to ensure that our design met the specified technical requirements and adhered to safety standards. ACTION: To start things off we organized a meeting where we discussed the project requirements and divided the tasks based on each member's strengths. This task consisted in relation to the shafts, gears and casing. Having said that, I created a detailed project timeline with key milestones and deadlines. I scheduled regular meetings to review progress, discuss any issues, and reassign tasks if necessary since one of our team member had been operated recently. These meetings helped keep everyone accountable and allowed us to address problems. I also propose the idea to upload all the files in a google drive such as excel files, CREO design, manufacturing drawings and reports so that all the team members could edit and have access to all the material and be aware of the process. When disagreements arose, I heled meetings of all team member's and listen to their perspective and find a compromise. For instance, there was a debate about the gear ratio to use for optimal performance. I encouraged the team to conduct a comparative analysis of different gear ratios and make a data-driven decision. Apart from that there was a disagreement in regards to a team member that could not do his part in the time frame proposed. To solve this issue me and the other student his part and another part was assigned to the person that was absent. For last, I made sure to recognize and celebrate small victories to keep the team motivated. I also provided support when team members faced difficulties, whether technical or personal. For example, the team member that had been operated recently could not model his part in CREO since his hand was immobilized consequently I reach out to him and helped him with his part.
result: As a result of these actions, our team successfully completed the gearbox design project. The gearbox was tested and performed efficiently, meeting all the technical specifications and safety standards. Our team received positive feedback from our professors and classmates. I often felt the weight of responsibility, especially when conflicts arose or when we hit technical roadblocks. However, as we progressed through the project, I began to appreciate the value of systematic planning and collaborative effort. Organizing our tasks, having regular check-ins, and creating a supportive team environment gradually eased my initial anxiety. The positive feedback from our professors and the recognition at the engineering showcase validated our hard work and reinforced my belief in the power of teamwork and structured problem-solving.

This not only makes the project seem less overwhelming but also allows for more focused and efficient problem-solving. Secondly, I realized the value of clear communication and regular check-ins. I also learned that conflict, while challenging, can lead to better solutions when approached constructively. Facilitating open discussions and making data-driven decisions helped us navigate disagreements effectively. Thirdly, I gained a deeper appreciation for the iterative nature of design and engineering. Our initial ideas evolved significantly as we tested and refined our prototype like, placing the gears closer to the input and output shafts instead of further. This taught me to be open to feedback and flexible in my approach. In the future, I will place a stronger emphasis on planning and organization from the very beginning of a project. I will ensure that clear goals and timelines are established and that each team member understands their role and responsibilities. I will also foster a team culture where open communication and collaboration are prioritized, and conflicts are seen as opportunities for improvement rather than obstacles. Overall, this experience has reinforced my belief in the importance of structured, merit-based decision-making and the power of effective teamwork. By applying these lessons, I am confident that I will be better equipped to lead successful projects in the future.

situation: In my previous unit, ENGG2000/3000, students were assigned to a particular group within a team depending on their specialization (three groups: Structures, Motions, and Communications). As a mechanical student, I was placed in the ‘Structures’ group with four other civil/mechanical students. In my structures group, there were two students in their third year, and three second-year students (including me). For each of the three groups in a team, the third-year students were assigned as leaders of their group. As a result, we had two leaders for our group who were responsible for allocating roles and responsibilities out to the team. They were also responsible for preparing an agenda for each week’s SGTA and any meetings outside of class times. They also kept in regular contact with the tutors and unit convenors and importantly had constant contact with the other group leaders to ensure all groups were staying on track and sticking to deadlines. However, about week 5 our third-year students had to leave temporarily from university. One leader needed an important surgery and had to stay at the hospital for several weeks. The other leader had to go emergency trip overseas to see his family. As a result, we had no group leader so I filled the role of group leader and its associated responsibilities.
task_action: As a temporary group leader, I had to initially approach the other two group leaders (Communications and Motions) and explain the situation to them about the two third years who had to leave temporarily. I explained that they should direct all their messages to me and add me to the leaders’ group chat on both WhatsApp and Discord. In the weeks that followed I would send regular weekly update requests to ensure our team was meeting deadlines and staying on track with the schedule. I would at least once a week contact our group members individually and ask how they were doing their sections and if they needed any help or support. Also, as our group was down by two, me and the rest of the group had to handle more tasks to compensate for the reduced manpower. I had to prepare the team's agenda an extra week or two ahead to ensure we had sufficient time to complete the tasks. Further, I requested our group to conduct meetings (10-15 minutes briefly on Zoom 2 days after the SGTA) to discuss problems we might be having and get on top of it as soon as possible. Otherwise, members with issues would have to wait until the next SGTA to get proper assistance. Another aspect of being a team leader meant that I had to learn about everyone’s strengths and weaknesses. This was done by constantly asking questions to members about how they would do a certain task (their suggested approach would highlight their level of understanding and demonstrate if they would struggle with that task and might need assistance) or had a preference (this would signal strength). Being an effective communicator was very important in being able to organize tasks and assign them to members with minimal hiccups, streamlining the process of the project. Additionally, I would send weekly summarized text to the on-leave third-year members of the tasks done that week and the agenda for next week. This would not only keep them posted but also allow them to remind me of tasks that I may have neglected.
result: By the time the third-year students returned to class, we had almost completed the marble machine. They were updated about the progress the team had made and what was remaining on the to-do list. The marble cube was built but the testing needed to be conducted and documented as well as some aesthetic additions to the cube. My time as group leader was very important in our progress. My leadership kept us on track, and we were able to successfully finish the entire cube promptly. If I had not filled in for the group leader, there was a considerable chance of our team not completing the cube in time. My effective communication with the other group leaders allowed for a smooth transition without many disruptions.
pfr: Initially, I felt that I was not competent or ready to become a group leader so abruptly as it was such a substantial task given that I was never a group leader for a project of this magnitude. I thought that it required a personality who is naturally sociable, communicative, and approachable. I consider myself to be the opposite of these things. I am normally a quiet, shy, and conservative person who does not overly interact with the other students around me. As a result, being just a group member and being assigned tasks by the group leader was ideal and comfortable for me. Becoming a group leader abruptly caused considerable discomfort and anxiety. Simultaneously, as our original leaders had to leave, the necessity to fill and get the job done pushed me into this uncomfortable position. I had to get used to feeling uncomfortable and putting myself out there constantly communicating with tutors, unit convenors, workshop technicians, and all the members of the team. By the end, feelings of discomfort had subsided, and I had become accustomed to the roles and responsibilities of being a leader.
learning: Through this, it was clear that being an effective team leader is an immense responsibility that requires a lot of time and effort compared to a regular group member. By being put in a position of leadership abruptly, it highlighted that anyone could become a successful leader. Extroverted and open personalities do have a natural inclination towards being a leader as it requires constant and frequent communication with other people (requires a lot of soft social skills). Introverted people like me can also become effective leaders with consistent effort. Even though it is an uncomfortable position in the beginning, you will get more accustomed to interacting with people. With enough practice and time, team leadership is a skill that can be acquired by anyone with the right attitude and effort.

Through collaboration with peers, industry professionals, and international partners, I've gained insights into the challenges and opportunities of the global space market. Furthermore, my involvement in the Astra white paper provided an opportunity to research how the global space market is addressing global Earth-based challenges using space technologies. This experience highlighted the industry's incredible support worldwide and reinforced the importance of collaboration and knowledge sharing on a global scale. My involvement in the New Horizons Summit provided opportunities to network with professionals from around the world, gaining insights into global trends, challenges, and opportunities within the space sector. As the marketing manager for the summit, I facilitated discussions and interactions that highlighted the importance of global cooperation in advancing space exploration and technology.
result: As a result of these experiences, I've developed a deeper appreciation for the global space industry, through hands-on experiences, research, and participation at many industry events, I've come to realize that these insights extend beyond just the space sector. They have provided me with valuable exposure to the broader global engineering landscape, and the connections between various industries. As I begin to understand the global market trends and economic forces shaping the space industry, I also learn how these trends intersect with other engineering disciplines. topic: Equity and diversity in leadership and managment
situation: During this semester, I was involved in a project where our team was tasked with designing a parking structure for a new mixed-use development in an urban area. The project required us to consider not only the technical aspects of the design but also to ensure that it addressed equity and diversity in its leadership and management approach. Our team consisted of members from diverse backgrounds, which added a layer of complexity in terms of communication and decision-making.
task_action: Our main task was to ensure that the parking structure would be accessible and accommodating to all users, including those from marginalised groups. This required us to incorporate features such as wheelchair-accessible parking spots, clear signage in multiple languages, and amenities that catered to various needs and preferences. Additionally, we aimed to create a leadership structure within our team that promoted equal participation and leveraged the diverse perspectives of all team members. ACTION: To address these challenges, I initiated several actions: * FORMING INCLUSIVE COMMITTEES: I suggested forming subcommittees within our team focused on specific aspects of the project (e.g., accessibility, safety, sustainability). Each subcommittee was led by a member with relevant expertise or interest, ensuring diverse leadership. * CONDUCTING USER SURVEYS: We designed and distributed surveys to gather input from potential users of the parking structure, including people with disabilities, non-native speakers, and various age groups. This helped us understand their needs and preferences, which informed our design decisions. * FACILITATING OPEN DISCUSSIONS: I organized regular meetings where all team members could voice their opinions and contribute ideas. These meetings were structured to ensure that quieter team members had an equal opportunity to participate. * IMPLEMENTING FEEDBACK MECHANISMS: We established a system for collecting and integrating feedback from both our team and community stakeholders. This iterative process ensured that our design remained responsive to the needs of all potential users.
result: The result of these actions was a well-rounded and inclusive parking structure design that received positive feedback from both the community and our faculty advisors. Specifically: * ENHANCED ACCESSIBILITY: The design included ample wheelchair-accessible parking spots, ramps, and braille signage, making it easy for differently-abled individuals to navigate. * MULTILINGUAL SIGNAGE: Clear signage in multiple languages was incorporated to accommodate non-native speakers. * POSITIVE TEAM DYNAMICS: The inclusive leadership approach led to high team morale and effective collaboration, with each member feeling valued and heard. * RECOGNITION AND LEARNING: Our project was highlighted as a model for incorporating equity and diversity in engineering projects, and I personally gained valuable skills in inclusive leadership and project management. This experience underscored the importance of equity and diversity in engineering leadership and management. It demonstrated that when diverse perspectives are actively included, the outcomes are not only more innovative but also more relevant and beneficial to the community.
pfr: When we first received the task of designing a parking structure as a group we tried to focus on equity and diversity as well, I felt a mix of excitement and anxiety as I am an international student myself. The challenge seemed a little bit overwhelming as we had to deal with the technical complexities combined with the need to consider diverse user needs. Initially, I was concerned about how we could effectively integrate the principles of equity and diversity into a project that was traditionally seen through a purely functional and technical views As we progressed, however, relieved as our systematic approaches and inclusive practices were paying off. Collaborating with team members from diverse backgrounds was enlightening, as it brought forward perspectives and solutions I hadn’t considered before. Organizing inclusive discussions and facilitating feedback mechanisms not only improved our design but also fostered a sense of unity and mutual respect within the team. *
learning: This experience has been profoundly educational in several ways. Firstly, I learned that incorporating equity and diversity into engineering projects is not only possible but also enhances the overall outcome. By actively seeking input from diverse users and team members, we were able to create a more comprehensive and user-friendly design. This process taught me the importance of empathy and active listening in engineering – understanding the real needs of users leads to better solutions. Secondly, I realized the value of structured and inclusive decision-making. Forming subcommittees and organizing regular open discussions ensured that all voices were heard, and this inclusivity resulted in a more robust and well-rounded project. Moving forward, I will continue to advocate for and implement these practices in future projects. I now understand that leadership is not just about directing but also about creating an environment where everyone feels valued and empowered to contribute. Finally, this project highlighted the importance of adaptability and continuous learning. The feedback loops we established allowed us to refine our design continuously, ensuring it remained aligned with user needs and expectations. This approach of continuous improvement is something I will carry forward, always remaining open to feedback and willing to make necessary adjustments to achieve the best possible outcomes. In future projects, I will prioritize establishing clear, inclusive processes from the start, ensuring that all team members and stakeholders have a voice. I will also continue to seek out and incorporate diverse perspectives, recognizing that these are crucial to developing solutions that are equitable, innovative, and effective. This experience has fundamentally shifted my approach to engineering design and leadership, making me a more empathetic, inclusive, and more effective.

During this first half of the semester, my group A8 have performed exceptionally well in getting to know each other and working together with each other in order to complete any assigned tasks, as well as gather ideas for our RGM Project.

We all made sure that each and every one of us was participating equally to complete the tasks, by assigning a person with a different role each week (either Minute Taker, Chair Person or Presenter), and also by checking up on each other to see whether or not that task was completed and if they needed any help with their task.

An important factor for all of us to successfully build our relationship as a team was for us to first get-to-know each other. This was approached by creating a Team Charter during our first workshop, in which we listed down our long term goals – such as achieving professionalism within our group, maintaining a positive relationship with each other, becoming better presenters and leaders, and upholding a level of high quality of work throughout the semester as a group – as well as our personal goals that we wanted to accomplish by the end of the unit – which includes: Contributing fairly to the group work, learning new skills professional/interpersonal skills from our team members and actively learning from each other.

By listing down these goals, we were able to all have the same common purpose. This gave us a sense of direction of how we would all work together and gave us responsibilities that we needed to fulfil.

Regularly reviewing our group’s performance during our past workshops with our tutors was also a factor that lead to forming an effective team. After the presenter of our group has presented their work to the tutor room, our Minute Taker would record down the feedback given to us. Along with this feedback, the feedback given for our team reflection and minutes would also be collected and with all of this, we would look over them and discuss how we could improve for the upcoming weeks.

This technique has significantly improved our presentations later on in the semester, as we were more confident and prepared, however, we did not bring as-much significance in this technique for our Minutes. We should have focused more on improving our Minutes for each week, in order to achieve our best possible outcome.

Another thing our group could improve on, in order for us to be an effective team, is by giving us each other rewards, or words of compliments. Overall, my group has performed well in showing how we can form an effective team, with our strengths being communication, maintaining a weekly schedule and contributing fairly to the group work.

This included a Google Doc file for who would be taking minutes, presenting, and chairing each meeting throughout the project. We also made multiple tables in Miro, including a table for roles in guided brainstorming sessions and what individuals would be responsible for building specific events in the RGM. Secondly, we took various measures to assign these roles and responsibilities fairly and effectively. result: As a result of fairly, openly, and effectively assigning roles and responsibilities in this engineering project, our team was able to clearly see what tasks they had to complete, work on the tasks best suited to them, and were not upset at anyone for taking on a lesser workload. These factors have allowed us to work cohesively and complete our tasks as efficiently as possible. Examples of the effectiveness of our assignment of roles and responsibilities include having helpful brainstorming sessions where one person focuses on directing the session and the rest focus on brainstorming ideas, everyone knowing ahead of time what their roles will be in our weekly SGTAs, and everyone being able to successfully build their own self-selected parts of the RGM.
pfr: I personally feel our team has done a great job in assigning and fulfilling our roles and responsibilities, as everyone has been able to see what they need to do, everyone has had an equal workload, everyone has been able to complete their assigned work, and all our work has combined in a cohesive manner that has allowed us to keep up with the project workload. We analysed an issue where the pin might not pop the balloon, which was solved by sticking two pins together to make it more sharp and blowing up the balloon more so that the surface is thinner and easy to pop. This process allowed us to make judgements whether an event is worth executing and if it will actually work, which in this case worked and is now a part of our final RGM project.

Even though this was a smooth process, it was still daunting for me because it was hard to judge whether the events were going to work. As a team, we applied critical thinking by identifying issues and coming up with successful solutions and judging whether it was all appropriate to the event process. It allows us to not waste time on events that might not work and to focus on all possibilities that might occur in our events. It helped me become more positive and have a "We can do it" mindset. Along the way, I think as a group we can all agree that we learned to become more resilient to change and adapt as quick as possible to resume and progress with our work. situation: As part of ENGG1050, the students have been tasked with building a functioning Rube-Goldberg Machine (RGM) to perform a simple task. The machine is broken up into a number of sections, depending on the number of people in the group, so that each member is tasked with designing and constructing part of the contraption. There are a number of aims associated with this project, one of which is that the RGM must be reliable.
task_action: To ensure the RGM that I am a part of is reliable, my group has set a minimum standard that each component of each section must perform as required 9/10 times. If a component can not be modified to meet this degree of reliability, it must be removed from the machine and replaced with another, more reliable, action event. This guarantees that the machine as a whole is at least 90% reliable. ACTION: To meet this standard of reliability, each member of the group conducted testing of every component of their section 3 times. Each test consisted of 10 runs of the relevant event. The first test was conducted before any optimisation changes had been made. The second was conducted after making one adjustment to the component, and the third was conducted after all possible optimisation improvements were implemented. The number of times the action event was successful in each test was recorded and tabulated to make a graph of the change in reliability.
result: As a result of this rigorous testing approach, data was produced that greatly influenced the decision to keep or replace components in each section of the RGM. In each successive test for every group member, the reliability increased. In all but two components, the optimisation changes made allowed the event to function as intended at least 9/10 times. The data for the two components that did not reach 90% reliability drove us to replace these events. Further testing was conducted on the new actions to determine they performed at least 9/10 times. Overall, the RGM is now proven to be 90% reliable.
pfr: When we made the decision to only keep components that were 90% reliable after completing the optimisation process, I felt relieved. I was worried that tough conversations would have to be had with group members who wanted to keep events in their section that were not reliable. I was stressed that I would have to confront team members, who I had now become friends with, so the decision to follow what the tests communicated was very welcome by me. By letting the data drive our decision making, everyone knew that the choices made were practical rather than personal.
learning: From this situation I have learned that implementing data driven decision making is a great way to remove personal feelings from a situation and prevent individuals from feeling targeted. When everyone is aware that it is only numbers and statistics that influence the choices made, no one is made to feel hard done by when it comes time to make tough decisions. Furthermore, this way of reaching conclusions makes it easier to determine the best next step. As we all know, numbers do not lie. In future scenarios, I will remember what I have learned from this project, and be sure to implement numerical standards wherever possible to ease and destress the decision making process.

situation: I work as a steelfixer in construction, and despite currently pursuing a software engineering course, I have considerable experience in the construction industry, particularly with steel and rebar. This needed a solution that considered the entire construction process and the final use of the staircase. To solve the problem holistically, I: 1. Consulted the Team: Gathered input from the steelfixing team, site supervisor, and project engineer. 2. Analysed the Impact: Assessed how the misalignment affected the staircase's strength and the overall structure. 3. Redesigned the Rebar Layout: Adjusted the rebar placement and reinforced critical areas. 4. Implemented Checks: Established a step-by-step verification system for rebar alignment during installation.
result: The staircase rebar was realigned correctly, ensuring its strength and safety. The project stayed on schedule and the new check system improved our workflow, reducing the risk of similar problems in the future. situation: In week 2, the group had to create several conceptual designs to create a basic understanding of what we would like to include for our "Tea of Things" machine.
task_action: Brainstorming initial ideas and conducting background research. Starting with familiarising ourselves with everyone's engineering major and what ideas they included for their tea machine, a list of important functions was created based on the client's needs. This was analysed from last week's work where we filtered through different questions and how the client responded to each of them. We then took a short time apart to generate several simple concepts, including at least one important function and listing their key components. It is important that no idea was scrapped or deemed as "bad".* This is where the brainstorming session had gone awry. Instead of presenting ideas we just kept them to ourselves and had others say what was interesting about each of them, giving shallow feedback.* For the rest of the session, we conducted background research for our separate ideas or fleshed out the conceptual design that was most liked. I decided to do research on the different processes of making tea and the anatomy of a coffee machine to see if there was a way that I could bridge these two designs together.
result: In the end, I was able to get a rough idea of what my peers valued as important for their tea machines. I was able to get some feedback on three of my initial concept designs a "hopper system", a "spin/stirring mechanism", and a "teabag dunking arm". I found that the hopper system was my most popular design as it was a good delivery system that bridges gaps between other designs. From this as a launching point, I researched different tea-making processes and how a simple coffee machine works. I landed on tea infusion which ditches the need for single-use tea bags and allows the use of loose tea leaves. Different designs use mesh to contain or plunge the leaves so they may release their flavours more efficiently as they are allowed to expand. This, and other useful information, is found on Reddit under r/tea. I also did some research on how coffee machines and coffee pods worked and found out that for the best blends, water is distributed evenly through the cross-sectional area of coffee pods. This is irrelevant to tea all that is needed is hot water to release flavour from tea leaves. Using information from this subreddit, I was able to learn that loose tea leaves provide the most variety of tea flavours and help reduce waste by avoiding the use of single-use paper tea bags.

I was able to connect the dots from one design and apply it to the "Tea of Things" system. I found that by being an active member of the group, I was able to steer discussions and communicate important ideas, concepts and sources for research for everyone's benefit. Because of this, I have found value in setting the group environment to communicate possibilities more fluidly and without the restraint of turning down so-called "bad" ideas. Even if ideas are shortsighted, important lessons can be drawn from that. Additionally, when discussion died down and I started doing individual work, researching the basic ideas of tea and coffee allowed me to think more creatively as I drew ideas from more sources. In future, I should spend some time to pause and research the key ideas and methods on how to make something and present my findings to others so they may draw more ideas from me or the information that I processed.

situation: In my ENGG2050 Engineering Design unit I explored various critical topics, one of which was "Ethics, Integrity, and Social Responsibility". A significant part of this exploration involved assessing real world scenarios where these principles were either upheld or violated. For the Case Study 1 assessment I was tasked to examine the Firestone 500 tires controversy. This case involved the manufacturing and sale of the Firestone 500 tire, which were found to be defective. Despite being aware of the defects, Firestone continued to sell these tires to the public and maximise profits. This led to numerous accidents, causing injuries and fatalities.
task_action: The primary task was to analyse the ethical breaches in the Firestone 500 case, understand the implications of these breaches on public safety and corporate responsibility, and propose solutions or actions that could have mitigated or prevented the negative outcomes. I was required to demonstrate my understanding of the ethical principles involved and apply ethical frameworks to evaluate Firestone's decisions and actions. ACTIONS: To tackle this task I followed a structured approach to breakdown, understand and analyse the situation entirely. 1. Research and information gathering: I started by researching the Firestone 500 case extensively. This involved reviewing supplied and external sources for reports, articles, and legal documents to gather a comprehensive understanding and adequate knowledge about the defects, the companys knowledge of these issues, and the subsequent impact on consumers. 2. Ethical analysis: I applied ethical frameworks to analyse Firestone's decisions. I evaluated the actions from the perspectives of the company and its shareholders, and the public/consumer perspective, while considering the consequences, duties and moral principles involves. 3. Identification of ethical breaches: I identified specific points where Firestone's actions violated ethical principles. key Breaches includes prioritising profits over safety, failing to disclose known defects and ignoring customer reports of tire failures. 4. Proposing solutions: I proposed several actions that could have been taken to address the situation ethically. These included issuing a recall as soon as the defects were identifies, transparently communicating with consumers about the risks, and implementing more rigorous quality control testing.
result: The outcomes of this reflective and analytical process was complex and had multiple aspects to consider. The key outcomes I received was: 1. Deeper understanding: I developed a deeper understanding of the critical role that ethics, integrity, and social responsibility play in engineering practices. This understanding was not just theoretical but grounded by real world implications and consequences. 2. Enhanced analytical skills: Through the detailed analysis of the Firestone case, my ability to critically evaluate corporate actions from an ethical standpoint improved significantly. I learned to apply ethical frameworks effectively to real world scenarios. 3. Awareness of impact: The task highlighted the importance of considering the broader impact of engineering decisions on society. It shows how lapses in ethical judgement can lead to severe consequences, both for public safety and corporate reputation. 4. Commitment to ethical practices: This case study reinforced my commitment to upholding ethical standards in my future engineering career. It served as a reminder that the welfare of the public should always take precedence over financial incentives. The case study 1 assessment on the Firestone 500 tire controversy was a profound learning experience that emphasised the significance of ethics. integrity, and social responsibility in engineering. By reflecting on this case, I gained valuable insights into the ethical dilemmas that engineers may face and the importance of making principled decisions to ensure the safety and well-being of society.
pfr: Reflecting on this case evoked a mix of emotions. Initially, I felt a sense of disbelief and frustation. It was difficult to comprehend that a company could knowingly endanger lives for financial gain. As i delve deeper, these feelings shifted towards a somber understanding of the gravity of ethical lapses, not just in engineering but the world as a whole, as financial stimulation is always the goal for companies and they will try to achieve it by any means often. There was also a strong sense of responsibility and determination to not only learn from this case study but to ensure such mistakes are not repeated in my future career.
learning: Looking back I realise how significant this case study was in shaping my understanding of professional ethics. This process of researching, analysing and discussing the Firestone 500 case highlighted the severe consequences of neglecting ethical considerations. It was an eye-opener to the real world impact of engineering decisions and showed the importance of maintaining integrity and social responsibility. After studying the methods of testing and seeing how thorough it can be, it was clear that Firestone cut some corners when it came to their testing. I was able to recognise that they could have explored more preventative strategies to foster an ethical corporate culture. This experience taught me several important lessons. It reaffirmed the necessity of always putting public safety above all else in engineering decisions. it also highlighted the importance of transparency and accountability in corporate practices. The Firestone case made it clear that ethical lapses not only harm individuals but also tarnish the reputation and sustainability of the company. I learned the value of ethical frameworks in guiding decision making processes by applying ethical frameworks to provide a structured way to evaluate the actions of Firestone and derive ethical solutions. If I were to encounter a similar situation in the future, I would advocate for immediate action upon discovering any defects or potential hazards, prioritising transparency with stakeholders. I would also push for the implementation of comprehensive quality control measures and ethical training programs within the organisation to prevent such issues from arising. This experience has instilled in me the importance of continuous self reflection and ethical vigilance. I now understand that maintaining integrity and social responsibility in an ongoing process that requires constant attention and commitment. Moving forward I will ensure the following: 1. Prioritise ethical decision making:in any professional role i will ensure that all decisions are made with a primary focus on safety, transparency and integrity. 2. Advocate for ethical practices: I will actively promote and support ethical practices within any organisation I am part of, including advocating for robust ethical training programs and stringent quality control procedures. 3. Engage in continuous learning: I will stay informed about ethical standards and the best practices in engineering, regularly revisiting and reflecting on real world cases to enhance my understanding. 4. Develop ethical leadership skills: I will work on developing my leadership skills that emphasise decision making and social responsibility, aiming to inspire and influence others to uphold these values.
